caseStudies.name: Contoso, Ltd.
caseStudies.text:
HOTSPOT
-
Case study
-
This is a case study. Case studies are not timed separately. You can use as much exam time as you would like to complete each case. However,
there may be additional case studies and sections on this exam. You must manage your time to ensure that you are able to complete all questions
included on this exam in the time provided.
To answer the questions included in a case study, you will need to reference information that is provided in the case study. Case studies might
contain exhibits and other resources that provide more information about the scenario that is described in the case study. Each question is
independent of the other questions in this case study.
At the end of this case study, a review screen will appear. This screen allows you to review your answers and to make changes before you move to
the next section of the exam. After you begin a new section, you cannot return to this section.
To start the case study
-
To display the first question in this case study, click the Next button. Use the buttons in the left pane to explore the content of the case study
before you answer the questions. Clicking these buttons displays information such as business requirements, existing environment, and problem
statements. If the case study has an All Information tab, note that the information displayed is identical to the information displayed on the
subsequent tabs. When you are ready to answer a question, click the Question button to return to the question.
Overview
-
Contoso, Ltd. is a US-based health supplements company. Contoso has two divisions named Sales and Research. The Sales division contains two
departments named Online Sales and Retail Sales. The Research division assigns internally developed product lines to individual teams of
researchers and analysts.
Existing Environment
-
Identity Environment
-
Contoso has a Microsoft Entra tenant named contoso.com. The tenant contains two groups named ResearchReviewersGroup1 and
ResearchReviewersGroup2.
Data Environment
-
Contoso has the following data environment:
• The Sales division uses a Microsoft Power BI Premium capacity.
• The semantic model of the Online Sales department includes a fact table named Orders that uses Import made. In the system of origin, the
OrderID value represents the sequence in which orders are created.
• The Research department uses an on-premises, third-party data warehousing product.
• Fabric is enabled for contoso.com.
• An Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 storage account named storage1 contains Research division data for a product line named Productline1. The
data is in the delta format.
• A Data Lake Storage Gen2 storage account named storage2 contains Research division data for a product line named Productline2. The data is
in the CSV format.
Requirements
-
Planned Changes
-
Contoso plans to make the following changes:
• Enable support for Fabric in the Power BI Premium capacity used by the Sales division.
• Make all the data for the Sales division and the Research division available in Fabric.
• For the Research division, create two Fabric workspaces named Productline1ws and Productline2ws.
• In Productline1ws, create a lakehouse named Lakehouse1.
• In Lakehouse1, create a shortcut to storage1 named ResearchProduct.
Data Analytics Requirements
-
Contoso identifies the following data analytics requirements:
• All the workspaces for the Sales division and the Research division must support all Fabric experiences.
• The Research division workspaces must use a dedicated, on-demand capacity that has per-minute billing.
• The Research division workspaces must be grouped together logically to support OneLake data hub filtering based on the department name.
• For the Research division workspaces, the members of ResearchReviewersGroup1 must be able to read lakehouse and warehouse data and
shortcuts by using SQL endpoints.
• For the Research division workspaces, the members of ResearchReviewersGroup2 must be able to read lakehouse data by using Lakehouse
explorer.
• All the semantic models and reports for the Research division must use version control that supports branching.
Data Preparation Requirements
-
Contoso identifies the following data preparation requirements:
• The Research division data for Productline1 must be retrieved from Lakehouse1 by using Fabric notebooks.
• All the Research division data in the lakehouses must be presented as managed tables in Lakehouse explorer.
Semantic Model Requirements
-
Contoso identifies the following requirements for implementing and managing semantic models:
• The number of rows added to the Orders table during refreshes must be minimized.
• The semantic models in the Research division workspaces must use Direct Lake mode.
General Requirements
-
Contoso identifies the following high-level requirements that must be considered for all solutions:
• Follow the principle of least privilege when applicable.
• Minimize implementation and maintenance effort when possible.

caseStudies.name: Litware, Inc.
caseStudies.text:
HOTSPOT
-
Case study
-
This is a case study. Case studies are not timed separately. You can use as much exam time as you would like to complete each case. However,
there may be additional case studies and sections on this exam. You must manage your time to ensure that you are able to complete all questions
included on this exam in the time provided.
To answer the questions included in a case study, you will need to reference information that is provided in the case study. Case studies might
contain exhibits and other resources that provide more information about the scenario that is described in the case study. Each question is
independent of the other questions in this case study.
At the end of this case study, a review screen will appear. This screen allows you to review your answers and to make changes before you move to
the next section of the exam. After you begin a new section, you cannot return to this section.
To start the case study
-
To display the first question in this case study, click the Next button. Use the buttons in the left pane to explore the content of the case study
before you answer the questions. Clicking these buttons displays information such as business requirements, existing environment, and problem
statements. If the case study has an All Information tab, note that the information displayed is identical to the information displayed on the
subsequent tabs. When you are ready to answer a question, click the Question button to return to the question.
Overview
-
Litware, Inc. is a manufacturing company that has offices throughout North America. The analytics team at Litware contains data engineers,
analytics engineers, data analysts, and data scientists.
Existing Environment
-
Fabric Environment
-
Litware has been using a Microsoft Power BI tenant for three years. Litware has NOT enabled any Fabric capacities and features.
Available Data
-
Litware has data that must be analyzed as shown in the following table.
The Product data contains a single table and the following columns.
The customer satisfaction data contains the following tables:
• Survey
• Question
• Response
For each survey submitted, the following occurs:
• One row is added to the Survey table.
• One row is added to the Response table for each question in the survey.
The Question table contains the text of each survey question. The third question in each survey response is an overall satisfaction score.
Customers can submit a survey after each purchase.
User Problems
-
The analytics team has large volumes of data, some of which is semi-structured. The team wants to use Fabric to create a new data store.

Product data is often classified into three pricing groups: high, medium, and low. This logic is implemented in several databases and semantic
models, but the logic does NOT always match across implementations.
Requirements
-
Planned Changes
-
Litware plans to enable Fabric features in the existing tenant. The analytics team will create a new data store as a proof of concept (PoC). The
remaining Liware users will only get access to the Fabric features once the PoC is complete. The PoC will be completed by using a Fabric trial
capacity
The following three workspaces will be created:
• AnalyticsPOC: Will contain the data store, semantic models, reports pipelines, dataflow, and notebooks used to populate the data store
• DataEngPOC: Will contain all the pipelines, dataflows, and notebooks used to populate OneLake
• DataSciPOC: Will contain all the notebooks and reports created by the data scientists
The following will be created in the AnalyticsPOC workspace:
• A data store (type to be decided)
• A custom semantic model
• A default semantic model
• Interactive reports
The data engineers will create data pipelines to load data to OneLake either hourly or daily depending on the data source. The analytics engineers
will create processes to ingest, transform, and load the data to the data store in the AnalyticsPOC workspace daily. Whenever possible, the data
engineers will use low-code tools for data ingestion. The choice of which data cleansing and transformation tools to use will be at the data
engineers’ discretion.
All the semantic models and reports in the Analytics POC workspace will use the data store as the sole data source.
Technical Requirements
-
The data store must support the following:
• Read access by using T-SQL or Python
• Semi-structured and unstructured data
• Row-level security (RLS) for users executing T-SQL queries
Files loaded by the data engineers to OneLake will be stored in the Parquet format and will meet Delta Lake specifications.
Data will be loaded without transformation in one area of the AnalyticsPOC data store. The data will then be cleansed, merged, and transformed
into a dimensional model
The data load process must ensure that the raw and cleansed data is updated completely before populating the dimensional model
The dimensional model must contain a date dimension. There is no existing data source for the date dimension. The Litware fiscal year matches
the calendar year. The date dimension must always contain dates from 2010 through the end of the current year.

The product pricing group logic must be maintained by the analytics engineers in a single location. The pricing group data must be made available
in the data store for T-SOL. queries and in the default semantic model. The following logic must be used:
• List prices that are less than or equal to 50 are in the low pricing group.
• List prices that are greater than 50 and less than or equal to 1,000 are in the medium pricing group.
• List prices that are greater than 1,000 are in the high pricing group.
Security Requirements
-
Only Fabric administrators and the analytics team must be able to see the Fabric items created as part of the PoC.
Litware identifies the following security requirements for the Fabric items in the AnalyticsPOC workspace:
• Fabric administrators will be the workspace administrators.
• The data engineers must be able to read from and write to the data store. No access must be granted to datasets or reports.
• The analytics engineers must be able to read from, write to, and create schemas in the data store. They also must be able to create and share
semantic models with the data analysts and view and modify all reports in the workspace.
• The data scientists must be able to read from the data store, but not write to it. They will access the data by using a Spark notebook
• The data analysts must have read access to only the dimensional model objects in the data store. They also must have access to create Power
BI reports by using the semantic models created by the analytics engineers.
• The date dimension must be available to all users of the data store.
• The principle of least privilege must be followed.
Both the default and custom semantic models must include only tables or views from the dimensional model in the data store. Litware already
has the following Microsoft Entra security groups:
• FabricAdmins: Fabric administrators
• AnalyticsTeam: All the members of the analytics team
• DataAnalysts: The data analysts on the analytics team
• DataScientists: The data scientists on the analytics team
• DataEngineers: The data engineers on the analytics team
• AnalyticsEngineers: The analytics engineers on the analytics team
Report Requirements
-
The data analysts must create a customer satisfaction report that meets the following requirements:
• Enables a user to select a product to filter customer survey responses to only those who have purchased that product.
• Displays the average overall satisfaction score of all the surveys submitted during the last 12 months up to a selected dat.
• Shows data as soon as the data is updated in the data store.
• Ensures that the report and the semantic model only contain data from the current and previous year.
• Ensures that the report respects any table-level security specified in the source data store.
• Minimizes the execution time of report queries.

questions.stem: Contoso needs workspace-level version control with branching for its Research division. Assume both Git providers are permitted by tenant governance and all connection prerequisites are met. Which TWO offered configurations use a supported Fabric Git provider?

options.text: Store at the semantic models and reports in Data Lake Gen2 storage.
Modify the settings of the Research workspaces to use a GitHub repository.
Modify the settings of the Research division workspaces to use an Azure Repos repository.
Store all the semantic models and reports in Microsoft OneDrive.

questions.explanation: B and C use supported Git providers, GitHub and Azure DevOps/Azure Repos respectively. A and D are file storage choices and are not the offered workspace Git integration configurations. The shared original case and source single-choice key are preserved separately.

questions.stem: As a Fabric administrator, you need a logical Research classification for the Contoso workspaces and their items in OneLake catalog. Keep their capacity assignments unchanged. Which grouping and documented current management route should you use?
questions.explanation: Use a Domain and manage it in OneLake catalog > Govern > Domains. Workspace assignment associates its items with the domain. Capacity is a compute assignment and the candidate keeps it unchanged. Tenant is the organization boundary, not the requested department classification. Entra admin center does not create Fabric domains.

questions.stem: Candidate revision: a Fabric Data Factory pipeline incrementally appends strictly increasing, append-only OrderID values from a source into an explicitly maintained Orders destination table. No updates or late lower-ID arrivals occur. After reading the committed destination MAX(OrderID), which end-to-end process is appropriate?

options.text: Filter source OrderID greater than the committed maximum, append those rows, and update the checkpoint only after a successful load.
Load source rows below the minimum destination OrderID.
Append all source rows after every refresh without a checkpoint.
Read the maximum ID but do not filter or copy source rows.

questions.explanation: Candidate adds the destination and append-only assumptions missing from the case. A maximum watermark must drive source filtering, loading and a successful checkpoint, not merely a query returning MAX. This variant is a pipeline exercise; it does not claim to repair Import semantic-model refresh by itself.
questions.gradedReason: Reconcile this derived pipeline variant with the original Import model requirement; verify pipeline activity and transaction/retry behavior before approval.

questions.stem: Which syntax should you use in a notebook to access the Research division data for Productline1?
questions.explanation:
The case study puts the shortcut **`ResearchProduct` inside `Lakehouse1`**, and requires that all Research division data *"be presented as managed tables in Lakehouse explorer"*. A shortcut created under the lakehouse's **Tables** area is surfaced as a table, so it can be queried by name with Spark SQL:

```python
df = spark.sql("SELECT * FROM Lakehouse1.ResearchProduct")
```

The OneLake shortcuts doc shows exactly these two forms side by side — `spark.read.format("delta").load("Tables/MyShortcut")` and `spark.sql("SELECT * FROM MyLakehouse.MyShortcut")`.

- **A** is the right *API* but the wrong *path*: the shortcut lives at `Tables/ResearchProduct`, not `Tables/productline1/ResearchProduct`. Productline1 is the workspace name, which is not part of the lakehouse's relative table path.
- **C / D** – `external_table(...)` is not a Fabric notebook construct at all (and C is missing a closing quote).
questions.gradedReason: R11 second-pass review not performed; retained R10 finding is a lead, not new verification.

questions.stem:
You need to assign permissions for the data store in the AnalyticsPOC workspace. The solution must meet the security requirements.
Which additional permissions should you assign when you share the data store? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

blanks.label: DataEngineers:
options: Build Reports on the default dataset
Read All SQL analytics endpoint data

blanks.label: DataAnalysts:
options: Build Reports on the default dataset
Read All SQL analytics endpoint data
blanks.answer: Build Reports on the default dataset

blanks.label: DataScientists:
options: Build Reports on the default dataset
Read All SQL analytics endpoint data

questions.explanation: R11 correction warning: sharing the lakehouse with Read all with Apache Spark does not grant writes. None of the original DataEngineers choices satisfies read/write plus no report/model access. Build must refer to an explicitly existing semantic model, not an automatically created default model. Do not use this original three-part key to grade. A replacement requires a complete least-privilege architecture and case-wide authorization review.
questions.gradedReason: Design and verify a scoped write architecture, revise all three subparts and shared case default-model assumptions.

questions.stem:
You need to create a DAX measure to calculate the average overall satisfaction score.
How should you complete the DAX code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

semanticVisuals.title: Original DAX template — fill both dropdown blanks
semanticVisuals.content:
Rolling 12 Overall Satisfaction =
VAR NumberOfMonths = 12
VAR LastCurrentDate = MAX ( 'Date'[Date] )
VAR Period = DATESINPERIOD ( 'Date'[Date], LastCurrentDate,
    - NumberOfMonths, MONTH )
VAR Result =
    CALCULATE (
        [Dropdown 1: aggregate expression],
        [Dropdown 2: period filter],
        'Survey Question'[Question Title] = "Overall Satisfaction"
    )
RETURN
    Result

questions.explanation: R11 warning: Survey[Response Value] and Survey Question[Question Title] are not established by the case tables Survey, Question and Response. A numeric response-grain score and active date/question relationships must be specified. Period is a date-table filter; LastCurrentDate and NumberOfMonths are scalars, not that filter. AVERAGEA of question text is not the desired score; averaging per customer would change weighting. No DAX candidate is approved until the schema and survey/response weighting are explicit.
questions.gradedReason: Complete current primary-doc section review, source screenshot/case checks and native fixture where material; then independently challenge every final option.

questions.stem:
You need to resolve the issue with the pricing group classification.
How should you complete the T-SQL statement? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

blanks.label: ______ (between  WHEN ListPrice <= 50 THEN 'low'  and  WHEN ListPrice > 1000 THEN 'high')

semanticVisuals.title: Original T-SQL completion template
semanticVisuals.content:
CREATE [Dropdown 1] [dbo].[ProductsWithPricingGroup]
AS
SELECT ProductId,
       ProductName,
       ProductCategory,
       ListPrice,
       [Dropdown 2]
           WHEN ListPrice <= 50 THEN 'low'
           [Dropdown 3: medium-price branch]
           WHEN ListPrice > 1000 THEN 'high'
       END AS PricingGroup
FROM dbo.Products;

questions.explanation: Candidate VIEW plus searched CASE centralizes the T-SQL classification. The repaired branch includes 1000 and excludes the low group boundary 50. The first two original third-blank choices both exclude 1000. FUNCTION, PROCEDURE and TABLE do not complete the supplied CREATE ... AS SELECT view template; COALESCE/IIF/SET do not complete the searched CASE structure. The Litware requirement about exposing this view in a default semantic model remains stale and unresolved.
questions.gradedReason: Run actual SQL boundaries and resolve case-wide model exposure; inspect pricing screenshot before source-fidelity approval.

questions.stem: What should you recommend using to ingest the customer data into the data store in the AnalyticsPOC workspace?

options.text: a pipeline that contains a KQL activity

questions.explanation:
Two lines in the case study decide this: *"Whenever possible, the data engineers will use low-code tools for data ingestion"* and *"Data will be loaded without transformation in one area of the AnalyticsPOC data store."*

A **dataflow** (Dataflow Gen2) is Fabric's low-code ingestion tool — Power Query in the browser, with a data destination — so it is the one that honours the stated preference.

- **A** – a stored procedure is T-SQL code, and it cannot reach the external CRM system in the first place.
- **B** – a KQL activity targets a KQL database for real-time/log analytics; the source here is a nightly CRM extract, and the destination is a lakehouse.
- **C** – a Spark notebook would work technically, but it is the *pro-code* option, which the requirement explicitly deprioritises.
questions.gradedReason: R11 second-pass review not performed; retained R10 finding is a lead, not new verification.

questions.stem: Which type of data store should you recommend in the AnalyticsPOC workspace?
questions.explanation:
The technical requirements for the AnalyticsPOC data store call for **"semi-structured and unstructured data"**, and state that files loaded to OneLake *"will be stored in the Parquet format and will meet Delta Lake specifications"*. A **lakehouse** is the Fabric item built for exactly that: Delta/Parquet files in OneLake, with both a Files area (any format) and a Tables area, readable by Spark and by T-SQL through its SQL analytics endpoint.

- **A** – "a data lake" is not a Fabric item you create; OneLake is the lake, and the lakehouse is how you use it.
- **B** – a **warehouse** is relational and fully structured. It has no place to put unstructured files.
- **D** – an external Hive metastore is a metadata catalog, not a data store, and Fabric does not use one.

The community is 100% on C.

refs.t: Fabric decision guide: choose a data store

questions.gradedReason: R11 second-pass review not performed; retained R10 finding is a lead, not new verification.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric warehouse that contains a table named Staging.Sales. Staging.Sales contains the following columns.
You need to write a T-SQL query that will return data for the year 2023 that displays ProductID and ProductName and has a summarized Amount
that is higher than 10,000.
Which query should you use?
A.
B.
C.
D.

options.text: WHERE DATEPART(YEAR, SalesDate) = '2023' · GROUP BY ProductID, ProductName · HAVING SUM(Amount) > 10000
options.code:
SELECT ProductID, ProductName, SUM(Amount) AS TotalAmount
FROM Staging.Sales
WHERE DATEPART(YEAR, SalesDate) = '2023'
GROUP BY ProductID, ProductName
HAVING SUM(Amount) > 10000

options.text: GROUP BY ProductID, ProductName · HAVING DATEPART(YEAR, SalesDate) = '2023' AND SUM(Amount) > 10000
options.code:
SELECT ProductID, ProductName, SUM(Amount) AS TotalAmount
FROM Staging.Sales
GROUP BY ProductID, ProductName
HAVING DATEPART(YEAR, SalesDate) = '2023' AND SUM(Amount) > 10000

options.text: WHERE DATEPART(YEAR, SalesDate) = '2023' AND SUM(Amount) > 10000  (no GROUP BY)
options.code:
SELECT ProductID, ProductName, SUM(Amount) AS TotalAmount
FROM Staging.Sales
WHERE DATEPART(YEAR, SalesDate) = '2023' AND SUM(Amount) > 10000

options.text: WHERE DATEPART(YEAR, SalesDate) = '2023' · GROUP BY ProductID, ProductName · HAVING TotalAmount > 10000
options.code:
SELECT ProductID, ProductName, SUM(Amount) AS TotalAmount
FROM Staging.Sales
WHERE DATEPART(YEAR, SalesDate) = '2023'
GROUP BY ProductID, ProductName
HAVING TotalAmount > 10000

questions.explanation: Candidate repairs SalesDate consistently in every SQL alternative. A filters rows before grouping and tests SUM in HAVING. B uses an ungrouped date expression in HAVING, C puts aggregate logic in WHERE and lacks grouping, D refers to a SELECT alias before alias binding in HAVING. No Warehouse query execution ran.
questions.gradedReason: Complete current primary-doc section review, source screenshot/case checks and native fixture where material; then independently challenge every final option.

questions.stem:
You have a data warehouse that contains a table named Stage.Customers. Stage.Customers contains all the customer record updates from a
customer relationship management (CRM) system. There can be multiple updates per customer.
You need to write a T-SQL query that will return the customer ID, name. postal code, and the last updated time of the most recent row for each
customer ID.
How should you complete the code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Candidate constraint: LastUpdated is unique within each CustomerID, so there are no latest-timestamp ties.

blanks.label: , x =  ______  OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerID ORDER BY LastUpdated DESC)

semanticVisuals.title: Original T-SQL completion template
semanticVisuals.content:
WITH CUSTOMERBASE AS (
    SELECT [CustomerID], [CustomerName], [PostalCode], [LastUpdated],
           x = [Dropdown 1] OVER (
               PARTITION BY CustomerID
               ORDER BY LastUpdated DESC
           )
    FROM Stage.Customers
)
SELECT CustomerID, CustomerName, PostalCode, LastUpdated
FROM CUSTOMERBASE
[Dropdown 2];

questions.explanation: Candidate aligns FROM with Stage.Customers and explicitly rules out tied timestamps. ROW_NUMBER partitions per customer and ranks newest first; WHERE X=1 selects the latest row. LAST_VALUE and NTILE do not fill the shown row-number signature; the two aggregate alternatives do not correctly filter the computed rank.
questions.gradedReason: Complete current primary-doc section review, source screenshot/case checks and native fixture where material; then independently challenge every final option.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant.
You plan to create a Fabric notebook that will use Spark DataFrames to generate Microsoft Power BI visuals.
You run the following code.
For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

statements.text: The code embeds an existing Power BI report.
The code creates a Power BI report.
This call guarantees a predefined numerical summary-statistics table for every DataFrame column.

semanticVisuals.title: Fabric notebook code
semanticVisuals.content:
from powerbiclient import QuickVisualize, get_dataset_config, Report

PBI_visualize = QuickVisualize(get_dataset_config(df))
PBI_visualize

questions.explanation: Candidate distinguishes rendering a new temporary interactive report from embedding an existing report and from computing a guaranteed describe/summary statistics table. Expected No/Yes/No is proposed. Importing Report without invoking it does not embed an existing report. Exact QuickVisualize lifecycle/library version needs verification.
questions.gradedReason: Read current Microsoft powerbiclient QuickVisualize docs and execute notebook widget; check temporary/saved report lifecycle.

questions.stem:
You are the administrator of a Fabric workspace that contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1. Lakehouse1 contains the following tables:
Table1: A Delta table created by using a shortcut
Table2: An external table created by using Spark
Table3: A managed table -
You plan to connect to Lakehouse1 by using its SQL endpoint.
What will you be able to do after connecting to Lakehouse1?
questions.explanation:
Two facts decide every option here.

**1. The SQL analytics endpoint is read-only.** The doc states it plainly: *"The SQL analytics endpoint … is a read-only experience. It doesn't support the full T-SQL surface area of a Fabric warehouse."* You can `SELECT`, create views and apply security, but you cannot `INSERT`, `UPDATE` or `DELETE`. That kills **B** (update Table3) and **D** (update Table1) regardless of table kind.

**2. The endpoint only surfaces managed Delta tables in the lakehouse `Tables` area.** Spark **external** tables are registered in the metastore with their own `LOCATION`; they appear in Lakehouse explorer but are *not* projected into the SQL analytics endpoint. That kills **C**.

**Table3 is a managed table**, so it is exposed and readable — **A**. (Table1, the shortcut, is also readable, but the option offered for it asks to *update* it, which is not allowed.)

refs.t: SQL analytics endpoint for a lakehouse

questions.gradedReason: R11 second-pass review not performed; retained R10 finding is a lead, not new verification.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse.
You use a dataflow to load a new dataset from OneLake to the warehouse.
You need to add a PowerQuery step to identify the maximum values for the numeric columns.
Which function should you include in the step?
questions.explanation:
Read the ask precisely: the maximum values for **the numeric columns** — plural, across columns, in **one** Power Query step.

**`Table.Profile`** does exactly that. It returns one row *per column* with the columns `Min`, `Max`, `Average`, `StandardDeviation`, `Count`, `NullCount` and `DistinctCount` — so a single step yields the maximum of every numeric column at once.

- **B `Table.Max`** returns *one row* — the largest row of the table according to a comparison criterion you must supply. It gives you a record, not a per-column maximum, and you would need a separate step per column.
- **A `Table.MaxN`** is the same idea for the *N* largest rows.
- **C `Table.Range`** returns a slice of rows by position. Nothing to do with maxima.

*Note:* about a third of the community votes B, arguing that "profiling" is a pane in the UI rather than a step. But `Table.Profile` is a genuine M function that you can add as a step, and it is the only option that answers the question for all numeric columns at once.
questions.gradedReason: R11 second-pass review not performed; retained R10 finding is a lead, not new verification.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a machine learning model registered in a Fabric workspace.
You need to use the model to generate predictions by using the PREDICT function in a Fabric notebook.
Which two languages can you use to perform model scoring? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.
NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.
questions.explanation: C and D. Fabric documents notebook scoring through Spark SQL PREDICT and PySpark APIs using an MLFlowTransformer, including a Transformer or derived UDF route. The Spark SQL example uses SQLTransformer after model setup; a separate manually registered SQL UDF is not universally required. Warehouse T-SQL and DAX are not the documented notebook scoring languages for this task.

questions.stem:
You are analyzing the data in a Fabric notebook.
You have a Spark DataFrame assigned to a variable named df.
You need to use the Chart view in the notebook to explore the data manually.
Which function should you run to make the data available in the Chart view?
questions.explanation:
**`display(df)`** is the Fabric notebook function that renders the rich output widget — and that widget is where the **Chart view** toggle lives. The doc: *"You can use the `display` function … on Spark DataFrames … to produce the rich dataframe table view and chart view."*

- **B `show`** – `df.show()` prints a plain ASCII table to the cell output. No widget, no chart view.
- **A `displayHTML`** – renders an arbitrary HTML string. It is unrelated to DataFrames and gives you no chart view.
- **C `write`** – `df.write` persists the DataFrame to storage; it produces no output at all.
questions.gradedReason: R11 second-pass review not performed; retained R10 finding is a lead, not new verification.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a Microsoft Power BI report named Report1. Report1 includes a Python visual.
Data displayed by the visual is grouped automatically and duplicate rows are NOT displayed.
You need all rows to appear in the visual.
What should you do?

options.text: Reference the columns in the Python code by index.
Modify the Sort Column By property for all columns.
Add a unique field to each row.
Modify the Summarize By property for all columns.

questions.explanation:
Power BI aggregates the data it hands to a Python (or R) visual: identical rows are collapsed before the script ever runs. The documented workaround is to make every row distinguishable. From the *Tips* section of the Python visuals doc: *"In some cases, you might not want automatic grouping to occur, or you might want all rows to appear, including duplicates. In those cases, you can **add an index field to your dataset that causes all rows to be considered unique** and prevents grouping."*

Adding a field whose value is different on every row is exactly **C — add a unique field to each row**.

- **A** – *"Reference the columns in the Python code by index"* is about how your script addresses `dataset` columns. It changes nothing about the grouping Power BI has already applied before the script runs.
- **B** – *Sort Column By* controls display order only.
- **D** – *Summarize By* governs how a numeric column is aggregated in a visual (Sum, Average, …). Setting it to *Don't summarize* stops measures being summed, but the row-level de-duplication that feeds the Python visual still happens.

*Note:* the highest-voted comment (+73) answers **A** — but it quotes the doc sentence above, which describes adding an **index field** (a new column of unique values), not "referencing columns by index". A later comment (+13) catches the mix-up. The PDF key and 53% of the community are on **C**.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model. The model contains data about retail stores.
You need to write a DAX query that will be executed by using the XMLA endpoint. The query must return a table of stores that have opened since
December 1, 2023.
How should you complete the DAX expression? To answer, drag the appropriate values to the correct targets. Each value may be used once, more
than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

semanticVisuals.title: Original DAX query with draggable target markers
semanticVisuals.content:
[Target 1]
    VAR _SalesSince = DATE (2023, 12, 01)
[Target 2]
    FILTER (
        [Target 3] (Store, Store[Name], Store[OpenDate]),
        Store[OpenDate] >= _SalesSince
    )

questions.explanation:
**DEFINE — EVALUATE — SUMMARIZE.** A DAX *query* (the kind the XMLA endpoint executes, as opposed to a measure) has a fixed skeleton:

```dax
DEFINE
    VAR _SalesSince = DATE ( 2023, 12, 01 )
EVALUATE
    FILTER (
        SUMMARIZE ( Store, Store[Name], Store[OpenDate] ),
        Store[OpenDate] >= _SalesSince
    )
```

- **`DEFINE`** introduces the optional definition block. It is *"used to define entities that exist only for the duration of the query"* — here the `VAR _SalesSince`. It must come first, and a query may have at most one.
- **`EVALUATE`** is mandatory and introduces the table expression that the query returns: *"the EVALUATE statement … contains a table expression to be evaluated and returned."*
- **`SUMMARIZE`** is the missing function inside `FILTER`. `FILTER(<table>, <condition>)` needs a *table* as its first argument, and `SUMMARIZE(Store, Store[Name], Store[OpenDate])` produces the two-column table of stores that the filter then narrows to those opened on or after 1 December 2023.

- **`TABLE`** is not a DAX query keyword (it is a `DEFINE TABLE` sub-clause, which does not fit any of these slots).
- **`FILTER`** is already printed in the code, so it is a distractor in the Values pane.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that contains a dataflow named Dataflow1. Dataflow1 has a query that returns 2,000 rows.
You view the query in Power Query as shown in the following exhibit.
What can you identify about the pickupLongitude column?

options.text: All the table rows are profiled.
There are 935 values that occur only once.

questions.explanation:
Read the **Column statistics** panel in the exhibit for `pickupLongitude`:

| Statistic | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Count | **1000** |
| Error count | 0 |
| Null count | **0** |
| Distinct count | **935** |
| Unique count | **871** |
| NaN count | 0 |

**A — the column has duplicate values.** 1,000 values but only **935 distinct** ones, so 65 of them repeat a value already seen. Duplicates, confirmed.

- **B** – the query returns **2,000** rows but `Count` is **1,000**. Power Query profiles only the **top 1,000 rows** by default (the status bar offers "Column profiling based on top 1000 rows"), so not all rows are profiled.
- **C** – `Null count` is **0** and `Error count` is **0**. No missing values.
- **D** – 935 is the **Distinct count** (how many different values exist), not how many occur exactly once. The count of values occurring only once is the **Unique count**, which is **871**.

questions.stem:
You are creating a semantic model in Microsoft Power BI Desktop.
You plan to make bulk changes to the model by using the Tabular Model Definition Language (TMDL) extension for Microsoft Visual Studio Code.
You need to save the semantic model to a file.
Which file format should you use?
questions.explanation:
**PBIP — Power BI Project.** Saving as a project writes the report and the semantic model out as **plain-text folders on disk** instead of one binary file, which is what makes the model definition editable in VS Code and diffable in Git. The semantic model folder is where the **TMDL** files live (`definition/tables/*.tmdl`), so the TMDL extension for VS Code can open and bulk-edit them.

- **B PBIX** – the standard Power BI Desktop file. It is a single binary archive; external text tooling cannot edit the model inside it.
- **C PBIT** – a Power BI *template*: a PBIX without the data. Still binary, still not text-editable.
- **D PBIDS** – a tiny "data source" connection file used to start a new report against a given source. It contains no model at all.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse named Warehouse1. Warehouse1 contains three schemas named schemaA, schemaB, and
schemaC.
You need to ensure that a user named User1 can truncate tables in schemaA only.
How should you complete the T-SQL statement? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
**`GRANT ALTER ON SCHEMA::schemaA TO User1;`**

**The permission — `ALTER`.** There is no `TRUNCATE` permission in T-SQL. `TRUNCATE TABLE` requires, at minimum, **`ALTER` permission on the table**: *"The minimum permission required is ALTER on table_name."* Granting `ALTER` at the schema level covers every table in that schema, present and future.
- `CONNECT` only lets a principal open a connection to the database.
- `EXECUTE` applies to programmable objects (procedures, functions), not to truncating tables.

**The securable — `SCHEMA::schemaA`.** The requirement is *schemaA only*. Schema-scoped grants use the `SCHEMA::` class, and this scopes the permission to exactly one schema — schemaB and schemaC are untouched.
- `DATABASE::schemaA` is the wrong class *and* the wrong scope: it would name the whole database (and `schemaA` is not a database).
- `OBJECT::schemaA` scopes to a single object such as one table; `schemaA` is a schema, not an object.

*Note:* one commenter points out that Fabric Warehouse did not originally support `TRUNCATE TABLE`. That does not change the answer — the question is testing the GRANT syntax, and `ALTER ON SCHEMA::` is the least-privilege grant for it.

questions.stem:
You plan to deploy Microsoft Power BI items by using Fabric deployment pipelines. You have a deployment pipeline that contains three stages
named Development, Test, and Production. A workspace is assigned to each stage.
You need to provide Power BI developers with access to the pipeline. The solution must meet the following requirements:
Ensure that the developers can deploy items to the workspaces for Development and Test.
Prevent the developers from deploying items to the workspace for Production.
Follow the principle of least privilege.
Which three levels of access should you assign to the developers? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.

options.text: Build permission to the production semantic models
Admin access to the deployment pipeline
Viewer access to the Development and Test workspaces
Viewer access to the Production workspace
Contributor access to the Development and Test workspaces
Contributor access to the Production workspace

questions.explanation:
Deployment pipelines need permission in **two** places: on the **pipeline** (to see and operate it) and on each **workspace** (to read from the source and write to the target). Least privilege then decides the level in each workspace.

- **B — Admin access to the deployment pipeline.** Pipeline access is a single role: users granted access to a pipeline get pipeline admin rights. Without it the developers cannot open or run the pipeline at all.
- **E — Contributor access to the Development and Test workspaces.** Deploying *into* a stage requires a workspace role that can write items — **Contributor** is the lowest such role, so it satisfies least privilege while still allowing the required deployments.
- **D — Viewer access to the Production workspace.** The developers must be *prevented* from deploying to Production but still need the pipeline to function. **Viewer** is read-only: they can see the Production stage and compare it, but any deployment into it is blocked. Giving them nothing at all would be an option in principle, but Viewer is the level offered and it is read-only.

Rejected:
- **A** *Build permission on the production semantic models* – lets someone build new content on a model; it has nothing to do with deploying and adds privilege without need.
- **C** *Viewer on Development and Test* – read-only, so they could not deploy to the two stages they are supposed to deploy to.
- **F** *Contributor on Production* – would let them deploy to Production, which is the one thing the requirements forbid.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model named Model1. Model1 uses Import mode. Model1 contains a table named Orders.
Orders has 100 million rows and the following fields.
You need to reduce the memory used by Model1 and the time it takes to refresh the model.
Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.

options.text: Split OrderDateTime into separate date and time columns.
Replace TotalQuantity with a calculated column.
Convert Quantity into the Text data type.

semanticVisuals.title: Orders fields
rows: Calculated column that multiplies Quantity and Price

questions.explanation:
Both goals — less memory **and** faster refresh — point at the same two culprits in the table: a very high-cardinality column and a calculated column.

- **A — split `OrderDateTime` into separate date and time columns.** VertiPaq compresses column by column, and compression collapses as cardinality rises. A `Date/Time` down to the second over 100 million rows is close to unique per row — the worst case for the dictionary. Split it and you get at most a few thousand distinct dates and 86,400 distinct times, both of which compress hard. This is Microsoft's own guidance: *"split the column into separate date and time columns"* to reduce model size.
- **D — replace `TotalSalesAmount` with a measure.** It is currently a **calculated column** (`Quantity * Price`). Calculated columns are **materialised at refresh and stored in the model**, so they cost both refresh time and memory — 100 million decimal values of it. A measure is evaluated at query time and stores nothing. The guidance: *"calculated columns … increase the model size and can prolong data refresh time … consider a measure instead."*

Rejected:
- **B — replace `TotalQuantity` with a calculated column.** `TotalQuantity` is already a **measure** (see the Description column). This swaps the cheap thing for the expensive thing — backwards on both goals.
- **C — convert `Quantity` to Text.** Text columns are larger and slower than integers and cannot be aggregated. Strictly worse.

refs.t: Data reduction techniques for Import modeling

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse’. Lakehouse1 contains a table named Tablet.
You are creating a new data pipeline.
You plan to copy external data to Table’. The schema of the external data changes regularly.
You need the copy operation to meet the following requirements:
Replace Table1 with the schema of the external data.
Replace all the data in Table1 with the rows in the external data.
You add a Copy data activity to the pipeline.
What should you do for the Copy data activity?

options.text: From the Source tab, add additional columns.
From the Destination tab, set Table action to Overwrite.
From the Settings tab, select Enable staging.
From the Source tab, select Enable partition discovery.
From the Source tab, select Recursively.

questions.explanation:
The Copy data activity's **Destination** tab has a *Table action* setting with two choices, and their documented meanings decide this:

| Table action | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Append** | adds rows to the existing table, keeping its schema |
| **Overwrite** | **drops and recreates the table**, so both the schema and all the data are replaced |

The two requirements — *replace Table1 with the schema of the external data* and *replace all the data* — are exactly what **Overwrite** does, which matters here because *"the schema of the external data changes regularly"*.

- **A** *add additional columns* – appends constant/metadata columns to the source; it does not replace anything.
- **C** *Enable staging* – routes the copy through interim storage for throughput. No effect on schema or on replacing rows.
- **D** *Enable partition discovery* – interprets a folder hierarchy as partition columns when reading.
- **E** *Recursively* – reads sub-folders of the source path.

Note that *truncate*-style behaviour would not be enough even if it were offered: truncating removes rows but leaves the old schema in place.

refs.t: Copy activity in Data Factory for Microsoft Fabric

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a lakehouse.
You plan to query sales data files by using the SQL endpoint. The files will be in an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) storage bucket.
You need to recommend which file format to use and where to create a shortcut.
Which two actions should you include in the recommendation? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.

options.text: Create a shortcut in the Files section.
Create a shortcut in the Tables section.

questions.explanation:
Two separate constraints, both driven by "query … by using the SQL endpoint".

- **D — create the shortcut in the Tables section.** The SQL analytics endpoint only exposes what the lakehouse recognises as a **table**. A shortcut in the **Files** section is unmanaged storage: it is visible to Spark and to `OPENROWSET`-style file access, but it is not surfaced as a table, so the SQL endpoint cannot query it. Table-section shortcuts are auto-discovered and appear in the endpoint.
- **E — use the delta format.** The Tables area of a lakehouse is Delta Lake territory: *"The Tables section … only supports Delta Lake tables."* A folder is promoted to a table when it carries a `_delta_log`; a bare Parquet or CSV folder dropped into Tables is flagged as unidentified and never reaches the SQL endpoint.

Rejected:
- **A** – Files section, as above: invisible to the SQL endpoint.
- **B Parquet** / **C CSV** – neither is a table format on its own. Delta *is* Parquet plus a transaction log, so choosing delta gives you the Parquet storage anyway, plus the log that makes it a table.

*Note:* the vote is close (DE 50% / BD 44%), and the main dissenting comment claims *"Delta format not supported by S3"*. That is incorrect — Delta Lake is an open format that stores `_delta_log` alongside the Parquet files, and it works on S3 exactly as it does on ADLS. Amazon S3 is a supported shortcut target, so nothing blocks delta there.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1. Lakehouse1 contains a subfolder named Subfolder1 that contains CSV
files.
You need to convert the CSV files into the delta format that has V-Order optimization enabled.
What should you do from Lakehouse explorer?

Create a new shortcut in the Files section.
Create a new shortcut in the Tables section.

questions.explanation:
**Load to Tables** is the Lakehouse explorer command that converts files into managed Delta tables, and the doc states the output format outright: you can *"load **CSV** or **Parquet** data and keep output in **Delta format with V-order optimization**."* Both halves of the requirement — delta format *and* V-Order — are covered by the one action, with no configuration.

- **B / C — create a shortcut.** A shortcut is a *pointer*. It converts nothing; the underlying files stay CSV, which means a Tables-section shortcut would not even be recognised as a table.
- **D — Optimize.** `OPTIMIZE` compacts small files in an **existing Delta table** (and can apply V-Order while doing so). It cannot turn CSV files into a Delta table in the first place, so there is nothing for it to act on yet.

In Lakehouse explorer: right-click the folder (here `Subfolder1`) → **Load to Tables** → *New table*.

options.text: From the Destination tab, set Mode to Append.

From the Source tab, select Enable partition discovery.
From the Destination tabs, set Mode to Overwrite.

questions.explanation:
This is a UI-sequencing question: the partition column picker **does not exist** until the table action allows the table to be rebuilt. Microsoft's partitioning tutorial gives the order of operations verbatim: *"Expand **Advanced**, in **Table action**, select **Overwrite**, and then select **Enable partition**. Under **Partition columns**, select **Add column**, and choose the column you want to use as the partition column."*

The reason is structural: **partitioning is part of a table's physical layout**, fixed when the table is written. `Table1` already exists and is **unpartitioned**, so you cannot bolt a partition scheme onto it by appending — the table has to be dropped and recreated, which is what **Overwrite** does. Hence **D**, *first*.

- **B — select the partition column** is the *goal*, not the first step; the option is greyed out/absent until Overwrite is set.
- **A — Append** keeps the existing unpartitioned layout, so the partition option never appears.
- **C — Enable partition discovery** is a **Source** setting. It reads partitions *out of* a source folder hierarchy; it has nothing to do with how the destination is written.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a lakehouse.
You are using a Fabric notebook to save a large DataFrame by using the following code. df.write.partitionBy(“year”, “month”,
“day”).mode(“overwrite”).parquet(“Files/SalesOrder”)
For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

statements.text: The results will form a hierarchy of folders for each partition key.
The resulting file partitions can be read in parallel across multiple nodes.
The resulting file partitions will use file compression.

questions.explanation:
**Yes — Yes — Yes.** The code is

```python
df.write.partitionBy("year", "month", "day").mode("overwrite").parquet("Files/SalesOrder")
```

1. **Hierarchy of folders → Yes.** `partitionBy` writes **Hive-style partition directories**, one nested level per key in the order given:
```
Files/SalesOrder/year=2024/month=03/day=17/part-0000….snappy.parquet
```
Three keys, three nested levels.
2. **Read in parallel across multiple nodes → Yes.** Each partition directory holds one or more independent Parquet files, and Spark assigns files to tasks that run across the executors. Partitioned Parquet is precisely the layout that enables parallel reads (and partition pruning, when a query filters on year/month/day).
3. **Use file compression → Yes.** Parquet is compressed by default — Spark's `spark.sql.parquet.compression.codec` defaults to **snappy**, which is why the files are written as `*.snappy.parquet`. You would have to set the codec to `none` to get uncompressed output.

The community agrees (+39 on "yes yes yes").

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse.
Several times a day, the performance of all warehouse queries degrades. You suspect that Fabric is throttling the compute used by the warehouse.
What should you use to identify whether throttling is occurring?

questions.explanation:
The **Microsoft Fabric Capacity Metrics app** is the tool Microsoft points you at for throttling. It reports capacity units consumed, overage, carry-forward and the throttling state over time, so it shows both *whether* throttling is happening and *what* caused it.

There is also a decisive practical reason the alternatives fail. From the throttling doc: *"Just like most Warehouse operations, dynamic management views (DMVs) are also classified as background and covered by the Background Rejection policy. As a result, **DMVs cannot be queried when capacity is throttled**. Even though DMVs aren't available, capacity admins can go to **Microsoft Fabric Capacity Metrics app** to understand the root cause."*

- **C DMVs** – exactly the thing that stops responding during throttling.
- **A Capacity settings** – shows the SKU and its configuration, not live consumption.
- **B Monitoring hub** – lists item runs and their status. It can show queries are slow; it cannot tell you the capacity is throttled.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse.
A user discovers that a report that usually takes two minutes to render has been running for 45 minutes and has still not rendered.
You need to identify what is preventing the report query from completing.
Which dynamic management view (DMV) should you use?
questions.explanation:
**`sys.dm_exec_requests`** lists every request **currently executing**, with the columns you need to diagnose a stuck query: `status`, `command`, `total_elapsed_time`, and — critically — **`blocking_session_id`** and **`wait_type` / `wait_time`**. Those last ones answer "what is *preventing* the query from completing".

Fabric Warehouse supports a small set of DMVs for exactly this task; the monitoring doc's worked example joins `sys.dm_exec_sessions`, `sys.dm_exec_requests` and `sys.dm_exec_connections`, and it is `dm_exec_requests` that carries the execution state.

- **B `sys.dm_exec_sessions`** – who is connected (login, host, session state). It does not describe the running request.
- **C `sys.dm_exec_connections`** – the transport layer: protocol, client address, connect time.
- **D `sys.dm_pdw_exec_requests`** – the **Azure Synapse dedicated SQL pool (PDW)** equivalent. It is not one of the three DMVs Fabric Warehouse supports.

questions.stem:
You are creating a data flow in Fabric to ingest data from an Azure SQL database by using a T-SQL statement.
You need to ensure that any foldable Power Query transformation steps are processed by the Microsoft SQL Server engine.
How should you complete the code? To answer, drag the appropriate values to the correct targets. Each value may be used once, more than once,
or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

semanticVisuals.title: Power Query M completion template
semanticVisuals.content:
let
    Source = Sql.Databases("server.database.windows.net"),
    Database = Source{[Name = "db"]}[Data],
    Query = [Target 1].[Target 2](
        Database,
        "SELECT * FROM customer WHERE country IN ('USA', 'UK')",
        null,
        [ [Target 3] = true ]
    )
in
    Query

questions.explanation:
**Value — NativeQuery — EnableFolding.** The completed step is:

```m
Query = Value.NativeQuery(
    Database,
    "SELECT * FROM customer WHERE country IN ('USA', 'UK')",
    null,
    [EnableFolding = true]
)
```

- **`Value.NativeQuery`** is the M function that runs a native (T-SQL) statement against a source. Its signature is `Value.NativeQuery(target as any, query as text, optional parameters as any, optional options as nullable record)`.
- **`[EnableFolding = true]`** is the fourth argument, the options **record**. By default a native query is a folding *dead end* — Power Query cannot see inside your SQL, so every later step is evaluated locally. Setting this flag tells the mashup engine it may continue folding on top of the native query: *"you can indicate that you want to fold the transformations … by setting `EnableFolding` to true."* That is precisely the requirement, "any foldable Power Query transformation steps are processed by the Microsoft SQL Server engine".

Distractors: **`Table`** and **`Record`** are the wrong M namespaces (`Table.NativeQuery` does not exist); **`Optimize`** is not an M function; **`StopFolding`** is not a real option (and would do the opposite of what is asked).

questions.stem:
You need to create a data loading pattern for a Type 1 slowly changing dimension (SCD).
Which two actions should you include in the process? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.

options.text: Update rows when the non-key attributes have changed.
Insert new rows when the natural key exists in the dimension table, and the non-key attribute values have changed.
Update the effective end date of rows when the non-key attribute values have changed.
Insert new records when the natural key is a new value in the table.

questions.explanation:
A **Type 1** slowly changing dimension **overwrites** — it keeps no history. That single fact settles all four options.

- **A — update rows when the non-key attributes have changed.** This *is* Type 1: *"A Type 1 SCD always reflects the latest values, and when changes in source data are detected, the dimension table data is overwritten."*
- **D — insert new records when the natural key is a new value.** A key you have never seen is a genuinely new member, so it is inserted. Every SCD type does this; together with A it forms the complete upsert (MERGE) pattern.

Rejected:
- **B — insert a new row when the key exists and attributes changed.** That is **Type 2**: a second row per member, versioned. Type 1 updates in place instead.
- **C — update the effective end date.** Effective start/end dates are the **Type 2** validity window. A Type 1 dimension has no such columns, because there is no history to bound.

You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 and an Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 account named storage1. Workspace1 contains a
lakehouse named Lakehouse1.
You need to create a shortcut to storage1 in Lakehouse1.
Which connection and endpoint should you specify? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
**https — dfs.** The ADLS Gen2 shortcut dialog asks for a **connection URL**, and the doc gives its exact shape:

```
https://<account_name>.dfs.core.windows.net
```

- **Connection = `https`.** The shortcut is created over the storage account's **HTTPS REST endpoint**. `abfs` / `abfss` are the **Hadoop driver** schemes you use from Spark code to *read* a path — they are not what you type when creating the shortcut.
- **Endpoint = `dfs`.** ADLS Gen2 exposes two endpoints on the same account: `blob.core.windows.net` (flat Blob API) and `dfs.core.windows.net` (**Data Lake Storage Gen2 API**, with real hierarchical namespace support). Shortcuts require the **DFS** endpoint; `file` is Azure Files, a different service entirely.

Once the shortcut exists you address it inside Fabric with an `abfss://` OneLake path — which is what the `abfs`/`abfss` distractors are fishing for. One commenter who sat the exam reports the live item labels the first blank **"protocol"** rather than "connection"; the answer is the same.

questions.stem:
You are analyzing customer purchases in a Fabric notebook by using PySpark.
You have the following DataFrames:
transactions: Contains five columns named transaction_id, customer_id, product_id, amount, and date and has 10 million rows, with each row
representing a transaction. customers: Contains customer details in 1,000 rows and three columns named customer_id, name, and country.
You need to join the DataFrames on the customer_id column. The solution must minimize data shuffling.
You write the following code.
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
results =
Which code should you run to populate the results DataFrame?
questions.explanation:
A plain join of a **10,000,000-row** DataFrame to a **1,000-row** one triggers a *shuffle hash / sort-merge* join: Spark hash-partitions **both** sides on `customer_id` and sends every row across the network. That is the shuffle the question wants eliminated.

`F.broadcast(customers)` forces a **broadcast hash join**: the tiny DataFrame is copied once to every executor, and each executor then joins its local slice of `transactions` against the in-memory copy. The large side never moves. Microsoft's guidance: *"Broadcast hash join … avoids shuffling the large table, which significantly improves performance"*, and it is the recommended pattern when one side is small.

- **C** – the same join without the hint. Spark *may* broadcast it automatically if the table is under `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` (10 MB by default) and statistics are available, but it is not guaranteed — so it does not *minimize* shuffling by construction.
- **B** – C plus a `.distinct()`, which adds **another** full shuffle. Strictly worse.
- **D** – a `crossJoin` materialises 10 billion row pairs before filtering. Catastrophic.

You need to identify whether maintenance tasks were performed on Customer.
Solution: You run the following Spark SQL statement:
DESCRIBE HISTORY customer -
Does this meet the goal?
questions.explanation:
**Yes.** `DESCRIBE HISTORY` returns the Delta table's **transaction log as a table** — one row per commit, with `version`, `timestamp`, `userName`, and crucially **`operation`** and `operationParameters`.

Maintenance commands are ordinary Delta commits, so they appear there by name: `OPTIMIZE`, `VACUUM START` / `VACUUM END`, alongside `WRITE`, `MERGE` and the rest. Reading the `operation` column tells you directly whether maintenance has been run and when — exactly the goal.

```sql
DESCRIBE HISTORY customer
```

The default history retention is 30 days, so this answers "was maintenance performed recently". Compare the other solutions in this set: `REFRESH TABLE` (T1Q58) only reloads cached metadata, and `EXPLAIN TABLE` (T1Q59) is not even valid syntax.

Does this meet the goal?
questions.explanation:
**No.** `REFRESH TABLE` invalidates and reloads Spark's **cached metadata and cached data** for a table, so that subsequent queries see the current files. It is what you run after something outside your session has changed the table.

It returns **no result set** — nothing about past operations, nothing about `OPTIMIZE` or `VACUUM`. The command that exposes maintenance history is `DESCRIBE HISTORY` (T1Q57).

questions.explanation:
**No.** `EXPLAIN TABLE customer` is not valid Spark SQL — it simply errors. `EXPLAIN` takes a **statement**, not a table name (`EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM customer`), and even then it prints the **query execution plan**, which says nothing about whether maintenance was ever performed.

The command that answers the question is `DESCRIBE HISTORY customer` (T1Q57).

questions.stem:
You need to recommend a solution to prepare the tenant for the PoC.
Which two actions should you recommend performing from the Fabric Admin portal? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.

options.text: Enable the Users can try Microsoft Fabric paid features option for the entire organization.
Enable the Users can try Microsoft Fabric paid features option for specific security groups.
Enable the Allow Azure Active Directory guest users to access Microsoft Fabric option for specific security groups.
Enable the Users can create Fabric items option and exclude specific security groups.
Enable the Users can create Fabric items option for specific security groups.

questions.explanation:
Two tenant settings have to change, and the **principle of least privilege** (a stated Litware requirement) decides the *scope* of each: security groups, never the whole organization.

- **B — *Users can try Microsoft Fabric paid features* for specific security groups.** This is what lets the PoC team turn on Fabric capabilities. Litware already has the groups defined (`FabricAdmins`, `AnalyticsTeam`, …), and the PoC is explicitly limited to the analytics team.
- **E — *Users can create Fabric items* for specific security groups.** Without it the team can see Fabric but create nothing. Again scoped to the groups.

Rejected:
- **A** – the same setting as B but **for the entire organization**. It works, but it hands paid features to everyone — a direct least-privilege violation, and the security requirement says *"Only Fabric administrators and the analytics team must be able to see the Fabric items created as part of the PoC."*
- **C** – *Allow Azure AD guest users…* concerns external identities. No guests are mentioned anywhere in the scenario.
- **D** – the same setting as E but enabled broadly with **exclusions**. Deny-listing is the inverse of least privilege: anyone added to the tenant later is allowed by default. Allow-listing specific groups (E) is correct.

questions.stem:
You need to implement the date dimension in the data store. The solution must meet the technical requirements.
What are two ways to achieve the goal? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: Populate the date dimension table by using a dataflow.
Populate the date dimension table by using a Copy activity in a pipeline.
Populate the date dimension view by using T-SQL.
Populate the date dimension table by using a Stored procedure activity in a pipeline.

questions.explanation:
The technical requirement is specific: *"The dimensional model must contain a date dimension. **There is no existing data source for the date dimension.** The Litware fiscal year matches the calendar year. The date dimension must always contain dates from 2010 through the end of the current year."*

So the dates must be **generated**, not copied, and the table must be **extended each year**. Two tools can generate and load rows on a schedule:

- **A — a dataflow.** Power Query can build a date table from scratch (`List.Dates`, or a generated column set) and write it to the data store as its destination. Low-code, which matches Litware's stated preference.
- **D — a Stored procedure activity in a pipeline.** T-SQL generates the calendar (a recursive CTE or a tally table), the procedure writes the rows, and the pipeline runs it on a schedule so the current year is always covered.

Rejected:
- **B — a Copy activity.** Copy moves data from a source to a destination. There **is no source** — that is stated outright — so there is nothing for it to copy.
- **C — populate the date dimension *view* by using T-SQL.** You do not *populate* a view; a view is a stored query over existing data, and there is no underlying date data for it to select from. The wording alone disqualifies it.

*Note:* a few commenters object that the AnalyticsPOC data store is a **lakehouse** (see T1Q9), and a lakehouse's SQL analytics endpoint is read-only — no stored procedures. That is a genuine inconsistency in the question set; the exam still expects **AD**, and 89% of the community votes that way.

questions.stem:
You need to ensure the data loading activities in the AnalyticsPOC workspace are executed in the appropriate sequence. The solution must meet
the technical requirements.
What should you do?

options.text: Create a dataflow that has multiple steps and schedule the dataflow.
Create and schedule a Spark notebook.
Create and schedule a Spark job definition.
Create a pipeline that has dependencies between activities and schedule the pipeline.

questions.explanation:
The binding requirement is *"The data load process must ensure that the raw and cleansed data is updated **completely before** populating the dimensional model"* — i.e. ordered execution with dependencies between steps.

A **data pipeline** is Fabric's orchestrator. You lay out the activities on a canvas and connect them with **`On success`** dependency arrows, so the next activity does not start until the previous one has finished successfully. Schedule the pipeline and the whole sequence runs in order, every time.

- **A — a dataflow with multiple steps.** Steps inside a dataflow are transformations within *one* query, not orchestration across the separate load activities. A dataflow cannot sequence other items.
- **B / C — a Spark notebook or Spark job definition.** Both run code; neither orchestrates other Fabric items, and hand-rolling dependency logic in Spark would maximise, not minimise, effort.

semanticVisuals.title: OneLake access requirements
rows: Read all the SQL endpoint data.

questions.explanation:
**ReadAll — ReadData.** These are the three lakehouse sharing permissions, and the doc maps each to an access path:

| Permission | Grants |
| --- | --- |
| **Read** | open the lakehouse item — metadata only, no data |
| **ReadAll** | *"read all data using **Apache Spark** and OneLake APIs"* |
| **ReadData** | *"read data from the **SQL analytics endpoint** through T-SQL"*, subject to any SQL security policy |

- **User1** needs *"Read all the Spark data"* → **ReadAll**.
- **User2** needs *"Read all the SQL endpoint data"* → **ReadData**.

Plain **Read** is insufficient for either: it lets you see the item but returns no data. And the two are not interchangeable — ReadData does not grant OneLake file access, and ReadAll is broader than the SQL endpoint, so swapping them would break least privilege as well as the requirement.

questions.stem:
You have an Azure Repos repository named Repo1 and a Fabric-enabled Microsoft Power BI Premium capacity. The capacity contains two
workspaces named Workspace1 and Workspace2. Git integration is enabled at the workspace level.
You plan to use Microsoft Power BI Desktop and Workspace1 to make version-controlled changes to a semantic model stored in Repo1. The
changes will be built and deployed to Workspace2 by using Azure Pipelines.
You need to ensure that report and semantic model definitions are saved as individual text files in a folder hierarchy. The solution must minimize
development and maintenance effort.
In which file format should you save the changes?
questions.explanation:
**PBIP.** The requirement — *"report and semantic model definitions … saved as individual text files in a folder hierarchy"* — is a verbatim description of the **Power BI Project** format. Saving as `.pbip` produces:

```
MyProject.pbip
MyProject.Report/        definition/ …            (report pages, visuals)
MyProject.SemanticModel/ definition/tables/*.tmdl (model metadata as TMDL text)
```

Every artefact is a separate text file, which is what makes meaningful diffs, merges and Azure Pipelines builds possible — and it keeps development effort low because Desktop writes the structure for you.

- **D PBIX** – one binary archive. Git can store it, but every change is an opaque whole-file blob: no diffs, no merges.
- **C PBIT** – a binary template (PBIX minus data). Same problem.
- **B PBIDS** – a small connection-definition file that opens a new report against a data source. It contains no report or model at all.

*(Same fact tested from a different angle in T1Q22.)*

You are implementing a medallion architecture in a single Fabric workspace.
You have a lakehouse that contains the Bronze and Silver layers and a warehouse that contains the Gold layer.
You create the items required to populate the layers as shown in the following table.
You need to ensure that the layers are populated daily in sequential order such that Silver is populated only after Bronze is complete, and Gold is
populated only after Silver is complete. The solution must minimize development effort and complexity.
What should you use to execute each set of items? To answer, drag the appropriate options to the correct items. Each option may be used once,
more than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

targets.label: Bronze layer:  (items are "Pipelines with Copy activities")

questions.explanation:
**A schedule — An Invoke pipeline activity — A pipeline Dataflow activity — A pipeline Stored procedure activity.**

The question asks what should **execute each set of items that already exists**, so match each layer to the activity that runs *that kind of item* from the orchestration pipeline:

| Layer | Items you already built | Activity that executes them |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bronze | **Pipelines** with Copy activities | **Invoke pipeline activity** |
| Silver | Dataflows | Dataflow activity |
| Gold | Stored procedures | Stored procedure activity |

Chaining the three with `On success` arrows gives the required Bronze → Silver → Gold ordering, and a **schedule** on the orchestration pipeline makes it run daily. (A schedule is the *trigger* for the outer pipeline; it is not an activity you place inside one.)

**The PDF answer-key image is wrong on the Bronze layer** — it marks *A pipeline Copy activity*. The table states that the Bronze items **are already "Pipelines with Copy activities"**. Putting a bare Copy activity in the orchestration pipeline would mean *re-implementing* those copies by hand, leaving the pipelines you built unused — which directly contradicts *"minimize development effort and complexity"*. The **Invoke pipeline activity** exists precisely to call an existing pipeline from another one.

The community is emphatic: the three top comments (+30, +14, +8) all correct the key the same way.

- **A Spark job definition** is a distractor — no layer here uses Spark.

questions.stem:
You have an Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 account named storage1 that contains a Parquet file named sales.parquet.
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1.
Using a notebook in Workspace1, you need to load the content of the file to the default lakehouse. The solution must ensure that the content will
display automatically as a table named Sales in Lakehouse explorer.
How should you complete the code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

semanticVisuals.title: Original lakehouse table creation template
semanticVisuals.content:
df = spark.read.parquet(
    "abfss://fs1@storage1.dfs.core.windows.net/files/sales.parquet")
df.write.mode("overwrite").format("[Dropdown 1]") \
    .saveAsTable("[Dropdown 2]")

questions.explanation:
**delta — sales.**

```python
df = spark.read.parquet("abfss://fs1@storage1.dfs.core.windows.net/files/sales.parquet")
df.write.mode("overwrite").format("delta").saveAsTable("sales")
```

**Format — `delta`.** The requirement is that the content *"display automatically as a **table** named Sales in Lakehouse explorer"*. Lakehouse managed tables are Delta tables; writing the source `parquet` through unchanged (or `csv`) would leave files, not a table.

**Name — `sales`.** This is the key distinction from T1Q65: **`saveAsTable()` takes a table *name*, not a path.** The lakehouse resolves it to the `Tables/` area for you. Passing `tables/sales` or `files/sales` would be interpreted as part of the identifier and is wrong — path-style arguments belong to `.save()`.

| Method | Argument |
| --- | --- |
| `.saveAsTable(name)` | `"sales"` |
| `.save(path)` | `"Tables/sales"` |

*Note:* a handful of comments answer *tables/sales*, conflating the two APIs; the highest-voted (+46) and the answer key both give the bare name.

You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1.

questions.explanation:
The deciding constraint is *"must support **Power Query M formula language** expressions"*. Power Query M is the language of **Dataflow Gen2**, and a pipeline can run one through the **Dataflow activity**.

- **D Copy data** – the obvious choice for "copy CSV files to a lakehouse", and it is the answer to many similar questions. But Copy has no transformation language at all: it maps columns and moves bytes. No M.
- **B Notebook** – Python/Scala/SQL/R. Not M.
- **C Script** – runs a SQL script against a database. Not M, and it cannot read CSV files from storage.

So the M requirement, not the copy requirement, is what the question is testing.
