questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains lakehouse named Lakehouse1. Lakehouse1 contains a Delta table with eight columns.
You receive new data that contains the same eight columns and two additional columns.
You create a Spark DataFrame and assign the DataFrame to a variable named df. The DataFrame contains the new data.
You need to add the new data to the Delta table to meet the following requirements:
• Keep all the existing rows.
• Ensure that all the new data is added to the table.
How should you complete the code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

semanticVisuals.title: Original Delta schema evolution completion template
semanticVisuals.content:
df.write.format("delta").mode[Dropdown 1] \
    .option[Dropdown 2] \
    .saveAsTable("table")

questions.explanation:
**`("append")` — `("mergeSchema","true")`.** Each requirement maps to one blank.

```python
df.write.format("delta").mode("append") \
  .option("mergeSchema", "true") \
  .saveAsTable("table")
```

**Blank 1 — *"Keep all the existing rows"* → `append`.** `overwrite` would replace them. `error` / `errorifexists` throw if the table exists; `ignore` silently does nothing — so with those, the new data would never land.

**Blank 2 — *"Ensure that all the new data is added"* → `mergeSchema = true`.** The incoming DataFrame has **two columns the table does not have**. By default Delta enforces the schema and the write fails. Schema evolution fixes it: *"Columns that are present in the DataFrame but missing from the table are automatically added as part of a write transaction when `write` … [has] `.option("mergeSchema", "true")`."* The two new columns are added and existing rows get `NULL` for them.
- `mergeSchema = false` is the default and would error.
- `overwriteSchema` is for *replacing* a schema — changing a column's type or name, or dropping a column — and it only applies with `overwrite` mode, which would destroy the existing rows.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric warehouse that contains a table named Sales.Orders. Sales.Orders contains the following columns.
You need to write a T-SQL query that will return the following columns.
How should you complete the code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

semanticVisuals.title: Required query output
rows: Return Weight if present; otherwise Quantity if present; otherwise 1
Return the lower of ListPrice and SalePrice; ignore NULL values in SalePrice

semanticVisuals.title: Source SQL answer template
semanticVisuals.content:
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, ProductID,
       [Dropdown 1] (Weight, Quantity, 1) AS ChargedQuantity,
       [Dropdown 2] (ListPrice, SalePrice) AS OrderPrice
FROM Sales.Orders;

questions.explanation:
**COALESCE — LEAST.**

```sql
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, ProductID,
  COALESCE(Weight, Quantity, 1) AS ChargedQuantity,
  LEAST(ListPrice, SalePrice)   AS OrderPrice
FROM Sales.Orders;
```

**Blank 1 — `COALESCE`.** `Weight` and `Quantity` are both nullable (see the schema), and the requirement is a fallback chain: use the weight, else the quantity, else 1. `COALESCE` *"evaluates the arguments in order and returns the current value of the first expression that initially doesn't evaluate to NULL"* — and it takes any number of arguments, which is what makes the three-item list work.
- `IIF` takes a boolean and exactly two results; it cannot chain three fallbacks.
- `CHOOSE(index, …)` picks by ordinal position, not by nullability.

**Blank 2 — `LEAST`.** You want the smaller of two values **on the same row**. `LEAST` *"returns the minimum value from a list of one or more expressions"*, row by row.
- `MIN` is an **aggregate**: it collapses rows into groups and would require a `GROUP BY`. This is the trap.
- `COALESCE` returns the first non-null, which is not the same as the smaller one (`ListPrice` is `NOT NULL`, so it would always win).

The visual query merge dialog offers the same set Power Query does:

| Join kind | Returns |
| --- | --- |
| Inner | only rows that match in both |
| Left outer | all from the left, matches from the right |
| Right outer | all from the right, matches from the left |
| **Full outer** | **all rows from both** |
| Left anti | only left rows with no match |
| Right anti | only right rows with no match |

questions.stem:
You are implementing two dimension tables named Customers and Products in a Fabric warehouse.
You need to use slowly changing dimension (SCD) to manage the versioning of data. The solution must meet the requirements shown in the
following table.
Which type of SCD should you use for each table? To answer, drag the appropriate SCD types to the correct tables. Each SCD type may be used
once, more than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

targets.label: Customers — "Create a new version of the row."
Products — "Overwrite the existing value in the latest row."

semanticVisuals.title: SCD requirements
rows: Create a new version of the row.
Overwrite the existing value in the latest row.

questions.explanation:
**Customers → Type 2, Products → Type 1.** The change action named in the requirements table *is* the definition of the SCD type:

| Type | Behaviour on change |
| --- | --- |
| Type 0 | ignore the change — the attribute is fixed forever |
| **Type 1** | **overwrite the existing value; no history kept** |
| **Type 2** | **insert a new row (a new version), and close off the old one** |
| Type 3 | keep a "previous value" column alongside the current one — one step of history, not a new row |

- **Customers — "Create a new version of the row"** → **Type 2**. New rows, typically with a surrogate key plus effective start/end dates or an *is-current* flag, so the full history is queryable.
- **Products — "Overwrite the existing value in the latest row"** → **Type 1**. *"A Type 1 SCD always reflects the latest values, and when changes in source data are detected, the dimension table data is overwritten."*

Type 0 and Type 3 are distractors: neither matches a stated action.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 and an Azure SQL database.
You plan to create a dataflow that will read data from the database, and then transform the data by performing an inner join.
You need to ignore spaces in the values when performing the inner join. The solution must minimize development effort.
What should you do?

options.text: Append the queries by using fuzzy matching.
Merge the queries by using fuzzy matching.
Append the queries by using a lookup table.
Merge the queries by using a lookup table.

questions.explanation:
Two independent decisions:

**Merge, not Append.** *"Merge queries … creates a new query from two queries in a **join**"*; *"Append queries … creates a new query that contains all rows from a first query **followed by** all rows from a second query"* — a union. The requirement says **inner join**, so it is Merge.

**Fuzzy matching, not a lookup table.** The join keys differ only by spaces, so exact matching would drop rows. Power Query's **fuzzy matching** option on the merge dialog *"relies on … similarity"* rather than exact equality and is *"applied at the time of the merge operation"*. Its **Ignore space** transformation option does exactly what is asked, and it is a checkbox — which is what satisfies *"minimize development effort"*.

A lookup/transformation table is a manual mapping you have to build and maintain for every variation — far more effort. (It *is* an option within the fuzzy merge dialog, but it is not needed when a built-in option covers the case.)

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse named Warehouse1. Warehouse1 contains two schemas name schema1 and schema2 and a
table named schema1.city.
You need to make a copy of schema1.city in schema2. The solution must minimize the copying of data.
Which T-SQL statement should you run?

options.text: INSERT INTO schema2.city SELECT * FROM schema1.city;
CREATE TABLE schema2.city AS CLONE OF schema1.city;
CREATE TABLE schema2.city AS SELECT * FROM schema1.city;

questions.explanation:
**Zero-copy clone.** `CREATE TABLE … AS CLONE OF` creates a new table that **points at the existing Parquet files** rather than duplicating them. The doc: *"Microsoft Fabric offers the capability to create near-instantaneous **zero-copy clones** with minimal storage costs."* Only the metadata is written, so "minimize the copying of data" is satisfied absolutely — no data is copied at all.

```sql
CREATE TABLE schema2.city AS CLONE OF schema1.city;
```

Cloning across **schemas within the same warehouse** is supported, which is exactly this scenario.

- **D `CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT` (CTAS)** – the runner-up at 33% of the vote. It produces an independent physical copy: every row is read and rewritten. Correct result, maximum data movement.
- **A `INSERT INTO … SELECT`** – also a full copy, and it requires `schema2.city` to exist first.
- **B `SELECT * INTO`** – full copy again, and `SELECT … INTO` is not supported in Fabric Warehouse.

The clone is independent after creation: changes to either table do not affect the other, because Delta files are immutable and each table gets its own log going forward.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1. Workspace1 contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1 and a warehouse
named Warehouse1.
You need to create a new table in Warehouse1 named POSCustomers by querying the customer table in Lakehouse1.
How should you complete the T-SQL statement? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

blanks.label: Line 1
options: CREATE TABLE dbo.POSCustomers AS CLONE OF

semanticVisuals.title: Original CREATE TABLE AS SELECT template
semanticVisuals.content:
[Dropdown 1]
    DISTINCT customerid,
    customer,
    postalcode,
    category
[Dropdown 2];

questions.explanation:
**`CREATE TABLE dbo.POSCustomers AS SELECT` — `FROM lakehouse1.dbo.customer`.**

```sql
CREATE TABLE dbo.POSCustomers AS SELECT
  DISTINCT customerid,
           customer,
           postalcode,
           category
FROM lakehouse1.dbo.customer;
```

**Blank 1 — CTAS.** The body is a `SELECT DISTINCT …` list, so the statement has to be **`CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT`**.
- Plain `CREATE TABLE dbo.POSCustomers` expects a column definition list in parentheses, not a `SELECT`.
- **`AS CLONE OF` cannot be used here** for two reasons: cloning takes a table reference, not a `SELECT DISTINCT` projection; and the doc states *"Table clones **across warehouses** in a workspace are not currently supported"* — and a lakehouse is a different item again.

**Blank 2 — three-part name across items.** Within one workspace, a warehouse can read a lakehouse's SQL analytics endpoint by **cross-database query** using `item.schema.table`, hence `lakehouse1.dbo.customer`. `dbo.Customer` would look inside Warehouse1, where the table does not exist, and `dbo.POSCustomers` is the table being created.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant.
You are creating an Azure Data Factory pipeline.
You have a stored procedure that returns the number of active customers and their average sales for the current month.
You need to add an activity that will execute the stored procedure in a warehouse. The returned values must be available to the downstream
activities of the pipeline.
Which type of activity should you add?
questions.explanation:
Two requirements: execute a stored procedure, **and** make its result available downstream. Only **Lookup** does both. The doc: *"Lookup activity reads and returns the content of a configuration file or table. **It also returns the result of executing a query or stored procedure.** The output can be a singleton value or an array of attributes, which can be consumed in a subsequent copy, transformation, or control flow activity."*

Downstream activities then read it as `@activity('Lookup1').output.firstRow.<column>`.

- **The Stored procedure activity** (not offered here) would execute the procedure but **discards the result set** — which is why Lookup is the answer when the values must flow onward.
- **A Switch** – control flow branching on a value; it does not execute procedures.
- **B Copy data** – can *run* a stored procedure as a source, but it writes the rows to a sink rather than exposing them to later activities.
- **C Append variable** – adds a value to an existing array variable. It executes nothing.

*Note:* a commenter who sat the exam reports a live variant whose options are Switch / Copy / Script / Stored procedure — a different option set that would need a different answer. With the options as printed here, Lookup is correct.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains two workspaces named Workspace1 and Workspace2. Workspace1 contains a lakehouse named
Lakehouse1. Workspace2 contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse2. Lakehouse1 contains a table named dbo.Sales. Lakehouse2 contains a table
named dbo.Customers.
You need to ensure that you can write queries that reference both dbo.Sales and dbo.Customers in the same SQL query without making additional
copies of the tables.
What should you use?
questions.explanation:
The tables live in **two different workspaces**, and the requirement is a single SQL query over both *"without making additional copies of the tables"*. That is the definition of a **shortcut**: *"Shortcuts are objects in OneLake that point to other storage locations … Shortcuts allow you to reuse data **without copying it**."*

Create a shortcut in Lakehouse1 pointing at Lakehouse2's `dbo.Customers`; it then appears in Lakehouse1's Tables area and its SQL analytics endpoint, so `dbo.Sales` and the shortcut can be joined in one query.

- **C a view** – a view cannot reach across workspaces. Cross-database queries work **within** a workspace; to span workspaces you must create the shortcut *first* (and then a view over it, if you want one).
- **B a dataflow** – would copy the data into the target. Explicitly excluded.
- **D a managed table** – also a copy.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse.
You are designing a star schema model that will contain a customer dimension. The customer dimension table will be a Type 2 slowly changing
dimension (SCD).
You need to recommend which columns to add to the table. The columns must NOT already exist in the source.
Which three types of columns should you recommend? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.

options.text: an effective end date and time
an effective start date and time

questions.explanation:
A **Type 2** dimension keeps history by inserting a **new row** each time a tracked attribute changes. That forces three columns that do not exist in the source system:

- **D — a surrogate key.** Once the same customer has several rows, the natural key is no longer unique, so it can no longer be the primary key. A model-generated surrogate key restores uniqueness and is what the fact table points at, so each fact row is tied to the version of the customer that was current at the time.
- **E — an effective start date and time** and **C — an effective end date and time.** These bound the validity window of each version, so you can answer "what did this customer look like on date X".

Rejected:
- **B — a natural key.** It comes *from* the source (the business key, e.g. `CustomerID`). It must be carried into the dimension, but it is not something you *add* — and the question says the columns *"must NOT already exist in the source"*.
- **A — a foreign key.** Foreign keys live in the **fact** table, pointing at the dimension. A dimension in a star schema does not carry one (that would be snowflaking).

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant.
You plan to create a data pipeline named Pipeline1. Pipeline1 will include two activities that will execute in sequence.
You need to ensure that a failure of the first activity will NOT block the second activity.
Which conditional path should you configure between the first activity and the second activity?
questions.explanation:
Pipeline activities are wired together with **conditional paths**, and each one is a different promise about when the next activity runs:

| Path | Runs the next activity when the first… |
| --- | --- |
| On success | succeeded |
| On fail | failed |
| On skip | was skipped |
| **On completion** | **finished — success *or* failure** |

The requirement is that *"a failure of the first activity will NOT block the second activity"* — the second must run either way. That is **Upon Completion**.

- **A Upon Failure** inverts the problem: the second activity would run *only* if the first failed, and would be skipped when it succeeded.
- **C / D Upon Skip** (listed twice — a typo in the question) fires only when the first activity was itself skipped, which is not the case here.

questions.stem:
You have a Microsoft Power BI semantic model.
You plan to implement calculation groups.
You need to create a calculation item that will change the context from the selected date to month-to-date (MTD).
How should you complete the DAX expression? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

semanticVisuals.title: Original month-to-date calculation item template
semanticVisuals.content:
[Dropdown 1] (
    [Dropdown 2] (),
    DATESMTD ( 'Date'[Date] )
)

questions.explanation:
**CALCULATE — SELECTEDMEASURE.** The finished calculation item is the standard MTD pattern:

```dax
CALCULATE (
    SELECTEDMEASURE (),
    DATESMTD ( 'Date'[Date] )
)
```

**Blank 1 — `CALCULATE`.** Changing the filter context is what `CALCULATE` does: it evaluates its first argument under the filters given in the remaining arguments. Here that filter is `DATESMTD`, which returns the month-to-date set of dates.
- `GENERATE` produces a cross-join style table; `MEASURE` is a DAX-query keyword for defining a measure, not an expression.

**Blank 2 — `SELECTEDMEASURE()`.** A calculation item must work with *whatever measure the user puts in the visual*. `SELECTEDMEASURE` is the placeholder for it: it *"returns a reference to the measure that is currently in context when a calculation item is being evaluated"*, and the engine substitutes the real measure at query time. Without it the item could only ever transform one hard-coded measure.
- `SELECTEDVALUE` returns a scalar from a *column* when exactly one value is filtered — unrelated.
- `COMBINEVALUES` concatenates values for relationship keys.

questions.stem:
You have a custom Direct Lake semantic model named Model1 that has one billion rows of data.
You use Tabular Editor to connect to Model1 by using the XMLA endpoint.
You need to ensure that when users interact with reports based on Model1, their queries always use Direct Lake mode.
What should you do?

options.text: From Model, configure the Default Mode option.
From Partitions, configure the Mode option.
From Model, configure the Storage Location option.
From Model, configure the Direct Lake Behavior option.

questions.explanation:
A Direct Lake model can silently **fall back to DirectQuery** when data cannot be loaded efficiently into memory (guardrail exceeded, a view rather than a table, RLS on the warehouse, and so on). The switch that governs this is the model-level **`DirectLakeBehavior`** property, exposed in Tabular Editor as **Direct Lake Behavior** on the Model node:

| Value | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `Automatic` (default) | Direct Lake, falling back to DirectQuery when needed |
| **`DirectLakeOnly`** | **Direct Lake only — a query that cannot use it fails instead of falling back** |
| `DirectQueryOnly` | always DirectQuery |

To guarantee that *"their queries always use Direct Lake mode"*, set it to **Direct Lake only**.

- **B Partitions → Mode** – a Direct Lake table has a single `DirectLake` partition; this does not control fallback.
- **A Model → Default Mode** – sets the storage mode for *new* tables, not the fallback policy.
- **C Model → Storage Location** – where the model data sits. Unrelated.

following tables:

You need to modify the model to ensure that users assigned the SalesRegionManager role cannot see a column named Address in SalesAddress.
Which three actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and

Set Object Level Security to None for SalesRegionManager.

targets.answer: Open the model in Tabular Editor.

targets.label: Step 2
targets.answer: Select the Address column in SalesAddress.

targets.label: Step 3
targets.answer: Set Object Level Security to None for SalesRegionManager.

questions.explanation:
Hiding a column *from a specific role* is **object-level security (OLS)**, and OLS is per-role metadata you cannot author in Power BI Desktop.

1. **Open the model in Tabular Editor.** The doc: *"To create roles on Power BI Desktop semantic models, use external tools such as Tabular Editor."* Desktop can create RLS roles and DAX filters, but not OLS.
2. **Select the Address column in SalesAddress.** OLS is set on the object being secured, under the role's *Table Permissions*.
3. **Set Object Level Security to `None` for SalesRegionManager.** The two values are documented as:

| OLS value | Effect for that role |
| --- | --- |
| `Read` | the table or column is **visible** |
| **`None`** | **OLS is enforced — the table or column is hidden from that role**; to its members it is as if the object does not exist |

Rejected steps:
- **Set the Hidden property to True** – hides the column from the field list **for everyone**, in every role, and it is only cosmetic: the column is still queryable. It secures nothing.
- **Set OLS to `Default`** – inherits, which leaves the column visible.

questions.stem:
You have a Microsoft Power BI semantic model that contains measures. The measures use multiple CALCULATE functions and a FILTER function.
You are evaluating the performance of the measures.
In which use case will replacing the FILTER function with the KEEPFILTERS function reduce execution time?

options.text: when the FILTER function uses a nested calculate function
when the FILTER function references a measure
when the FILTER function references columns from multiple tables
when the FILTER function references a column from a single table that uses Import mode

questions.explanation:
Microsoft's DAX best-practice article *Avoid using FILTER as a filter argument* explains the optimisation. A filter argument to `CALCULATE` can be written either as a **table expression** (`FILTER(...)`) or as a **Boolean expression** — and the Boolean form is faster, because the engine can push it down as a simple predicate instead of materialising and iterating a table. `KEEPFILTERS` is how you keep the intersect-with-existing-context semantics while using the Boolean form.

But a Boolean filter expression carries documented **restrictions**. It:
- cannot reference columns from **multiple tables**,
- cannot reference a **measure**,
- cannot use a nested `CALCULATE`.

Options **A**, **B** and **C** each name one of those restrictions, so in each of those cases you *cannot* make the swap — `FILTER` is required. **D** describes the one case where the swap is both legal and beneficial: a single-table column reference. The article also notes it *"is especially relevant for model calculations that apply filters to **Import** tables"*, which is the rest of D.

refs.t: DAX: Avoid using FILTER as a filter argument

questions.stem:
You have a semantic model named Model1. Model1 contains five tables that all use Import mode. Model1 contains a dynamic row-level security
(RLS) role named HR. The HR role filters employee data so that HR managers only see the data of the department to which they are assigned.
You publish Model1 to a Fabric tenant and configure RLS role membership. You share the model and related reports to users.
An HR manager reports that the data they see in a report is incomplete.
What should you do to validate the data seen by the HR Manager?

options.text: Select Test as role to view the data as the HR role.
Filter the data in the report to match the intended logic of the filter for the HR department.
Select Test as role to view the report as the HR manager.
Ask the HR manager to open the report in Microsoft Power BI Desktop.

questions.explanation:
The word that decides this is **dynamic**. A dynamic RLS role filters on the *current user's identity* — typically `USERPRINCIPALNAME()` matched against an employee table. So the filter produces a **different result for every user**, and testing "the HR role" in the abstract tells you nothing about what this particular manager sees.

In the Fabric/Power BI service, **Security → Test as role** lets you select the role **and** enter a specific user to impersonate. Viewing the report **as the HR manager** reproduces their exact filter context, which is the only way to confirm whether the data is genuinely incomplete or the RLS logic is misfiring for them. That is **C**.

- **A — Test as role to view the data as the HR role.** This is the right *tool* with the wrong *scope*. With **static** RLS it would be enough; with dynamic RLS there is no single "HR role view" to inspect, because the filter depends on who is asking. 41% of the community picks this, reasoning that the role is named "HR", not "HR manager" — but the role name is not the issue, the identity is.
- **B — filter the report manually.** Reproduces what you *think* the logic should be, not what RLS actually does. It cannot validate anything.
- **D — have the manager open it in Desktop.** Desktop's *View as* does not apply the service's role membership, and the manager may not even have the model.

| Type | Question it answers |
| --- | --- |
| **Descriptive** | **What happened?** |
| Diagnostic | Why did it happen? |
| Predictive | What will happen? |

questions.explanation:
**DATETRUNC — weekday.**

```sql
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID,
  DATETRUNC(month, OrderDate)   AS PeriodDate,
  DATENAME(weekday, OrderDate)  AS DayName
FROM Sales.Orders;
```

**Blank 1 — `DATETRUNC`.** The spec is *"a date representing the **first day of the month** for OrderDate"*. `DATETRUNC` *"returns an input date truncated to a specified datepart"* — `DATETRUNC(month, '2024-03-17')` gives `2024-03-01`, a **date**.
- **`DATEPART`** returns an **integer** (`3`), not a date. This is the trap, and the distinction is what the question tests.
- `DATEFROMPARTS(y, m, d)` builds a date from three separate integers; it does not take a date as input.
- `DATE_BUCKET` snaps a date to fixed-width buckets from an origin — more machinery than needed, and not a month-start truncation.

**Blank 2 — `weekday`.** The spec is *"the **name of the day**, such as Wednesday"*. `DATENAME` returns a character string for the requested part, and the part that yields the weekday name is **`weekday`** (`dw`).
- `day` returns the day **of the month** — `DATENAME(day, …)` gives `"17"`.
- `dayofyear` gives the ordinal day in the year — `"77"`.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains JSON files in OneLake. The files have one billion items.
You plan to perform time series analysis of the items.
You need to transform the data, visualize the data to find insights, perform anomaly detection, and share the insights with other business users.
The solution must meet the following requirements:
• Use parallel processing.
• Minimize the duplication of data.
• Minimize how long it takes to load the data.
What should you use to transform and visualize the data?

options.text: the PySpark library in a Fabric notebook
the pandas library in a Fabric notebook
a Microsoft Power BI report that uses core visuals

questions.explanation:
Three requirements, and **PySpark in a Fabric notebook** is the only option that satisfies all three for **one billion items**:

- **Use parallel processing.** Spark distributes work across the executors of the pool. This alone eliminates **B**: pandas is **single-node, single-threaded** and holds the whole frame in one machine's memory — a billion rows will not fit, let alone run in parallel.
- **Minimize duplication of data.** Spark reads the JSON in OneLake in place. A Power BI Import model would copy it; a DirectQuery model over raw JSON files is not viable.
- **Transform *and* visualize, plus anomaly detection.** A notebook does all of it: PySpark for the transformation, `display()` and the chart view (or matplotlib/seaborn) for visuals, and Spark ML / SynapseML for anomaly detection.

- **C — a Power BI report with core visuals** can visualise but cannot *transform* a billion JSON items, and core visuals have no anomaly detection over this shape of data.

*(The "share the insights" part is then handled by the notebook itself or by a report built on the curated output — it is not what distinguishes the options.)*

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model. The model contains data about retail stores.
You need to write a DAX query that will be executed by using the XMLA endpoint. The query must return the total amount of sales from the same
period last year.
How should you complete the DAX expression? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

semanticVisuals.title: Original last-year-sales DAX query template
semanticVisuals.content:
EVALUATE
VAR _LYSales =
    [Dropdown 1] ( [Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR ( 'Orders'[Order Date] ) )
RETURN
    [Dropdown 2]

questions.explanation:
**CALCULATE — `{ _LYSales }`.**

```dax
EVALUATE
VAR _LYSales =
    CALCULATE ( [Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR ( 'Orders'[Order Date] ) )
RETURN
    { _LYSales }
```

**Blank 1 — `CALCULATE`.** `[Total Sales]` is a **scalar** measure and `SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(...)` is a filter to apply to it. `CALCULATE(<scalar expression>, <filter>…)` is the function for that shape.
- `CALCULATETABLE` has the same semantics but takes and returns a **table**; `[Total Sales]` is not a table.
- `FILTER`, `SUMMARIZE` and `SUMMARIZECOLUMNS` all return tables and do not take a measure as a first argument. (A commenter with +58 notes the printed distractor `SUMMARIZE` is a common wrong pick.)

**Blank 2 — `{ _LYSales }`, and here the PDF answer key is wrong** (it marks the bare `_LYSales`).

`EVALUATE` is documented as taking a **table expression**: *"EVALUATE ( <Table> ) … The table expression to be evaluated and returned."* `_LYSales` holds a **scalar** — the output of `CALCULATE` over a measure — so `RETURN _LYSales` does not type-check. Run it and the engine rejects the query: *"The expression specified in the query is not a valid table expression."*

The braces are DAX's **table constructor**. `{ _LYSales }` wraps the scalar into a one-row, one-column table (`[Value]`), which is a valid `EVALUATE` operand and returns the number you want.

| RETURN | Type | Valid after EVALUATE? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `[Total Sales]` | scalar — and the *current-year* figure, not last year's | no |
| `_LYSales` | scalar | **no** |
| **`{ _LYSales }`** | **table (1×1)** | **yes** |
| `VAR` | a keyword, not an expression | no |

*Note:* the community comment that addresses this blank (+12) makes the same point. The two higher-voted comments only discuss blank 1.

ISEMPTY ( RELATEDTABLE ( 'Order Item' ) )

semanticVisuals.title: Original slow DAX query (line 4)
semanticVisuals.content:
EVALUATE
FILTER (
    VALUES ( Customer[Customer Name] ),
    CALCULATE ( COUNTROWS ( 'Order Item' ) ) > 0
)
ORDER BY Customer[Customer Name]

questions.explanation:
**No — the logic is inverted.** The original query is

```dax
EVALUATE
  FILTER (
    VALUES ( Customer[Customer Name] ),
    CALCULATE ( COUNTROWS ( 'Order Item' ) ) > 0   -- line 4
  )
ORDER BY Customer[Customer Name]
```

Line 4 keeps customers that **have** at least one order. The proposed replacement is

```dax
ISEMPTY ( RELATEDTABLE ( 'Order Item' ) )
```

which is `TRUE` when the customer has **no** orders. It returns the exact complement of the intended set — customers *without* orders. Wrong result, so it cannot "meet the goal" no matter how fast it is.

The missing piece is the negation: **`NOT ISEMPTY ( ... )`** — which is what T1Q108 proposes, and why that one is **Yes**.

*(`ISEMPTY` is genuinely the faster idiom: it stops at the first row instead of counting them all. The optimisation is right; the sign is wrong.)*

The only change from the original is `> 0` → **`>= 0`**, and it breaks the query on both counts:

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model named model1. The two largest columns in model1 are shown in the following table.
You need to optimize model1. The solution must meet the following requirements:
• Reduce the model size.
• Increase refresh performance when using Import mode.
• Ensure that the datetime value for each sales transaction is available in the model.
What should you do on each column? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

blanks.label: TransactionKey:  (cardinality 2,500,350,000 — 160 GB — incrementing surrogate key for fact table SalesTransaction)
options: Change the data type of the column.

blanks.label: SaleDateTime:  (cardinality 6,850,273 — 120 GB — datetime to the nearest second of when a sale occurred)
options: Change the data type of the column.

semanticVisuals.title: Largest columns in model1
rows: Incrementing surrogate key for fact table SalesTransaction
Datetime to the nearest second when a sale occurred

questions.explanation:
**Remove the column — Split the column.** Both columns are enormous because VertiPaq compression collapses as **cardinality** rises, and each needs a different fix.

**`TransactionKey` → Remove.** 2.5 billion distinct values, essentially one per row, costing **160 GB**. It is an *incrementing surrogate key* on a **fact** table — and a fact-table surrogate key has no analytical use: nobody slices, filters or aggregates by it, and no relationship needs it (relationships point *outward* to dimensions). Microsoft's data-reduction guidance says to remove unnecessary columns, and *"consider removing… a primary key column of a fact table"*. Dropping it is the single biggest win and speeds up refresh because there is that much less to encode.

**`SaleDateTime` → Split.** The third requirement — *"ensure that the **datetime value** for each sales transaction is available in the model"* — forbids removing or truncating it. Splitting into a **date** column and a **time** column preserves the full value while collapsing cardinality: 6,850,273 distinct datetimes become a few thousand dates × 86,400 possible times, both of which compress well. This is Microsoft's documented technique: *"split the column into separate date and time columns"*.

Rejected:
- **Truncate the data** on `SaleDateTime` would drop the time component, breaking the "to the nearest second" requirement.
- **Change the data type** on either column is marginal — the cost is the *number of distinct values*, which a type change does not reduce.
- **Remove** `SaleDateTime` violates the third requirement outright.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a data warehouse named DW1. DW1 contains a table named DimCustomer. DimCustomer contains the
fields shown in the following table.
You need to identify duplicate email addresses in DimCustomer. The solution must return a maximum of 1,000 records.
Which four T-SQL statements should you run in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate statements from the list of statements to the answer
area and arrange them in the correct order.

semanticVisuals.title: Query requirements
semanticVisuals.content: Identify duplicate email addresses using CustomerAltKey; return a maximum of 1,000 rows. Order the four available SQL statements into a valid query.

questions.explanation:
The finished query:

```sql
SELECT TOP(1000) CustomerAltKey, COUNT(*)
FROM DimCustomer
GROUP BY CustomerAltKey
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
```

`CustomerAltKey` is the email column (see the sample data). Group by it, then keep only the groups that occur more than once — those are the duplicates.

Three distractors, each testing a specific rule:
- **`LIMIT 1000`** – `LIMIT` is MySQL/PostgreSQL/Spark syntax. T-SQL uses **`TOP (n)`**, which is why the row cap is baked into the `SELECT` line rather than appended at the end.
- **`SELECT CustomerAltKey, COUNT(*)`** – correct projection but no row cap, so it fails *"a maximum of 1,000 records"*.
- **`WHERE COUNT(*) > 1`** – invalid. `WHERE` filters rows **before** aggregation and cannot contain an aggregate function; filtering groups is what **`HAVING`** is for.

The clause order is fixed by T-SQL syntax: `SELECT … FROM … GROUP BY … HAVING …`.

**1. It is a scalar function → No.** *(The PDF answer-key image marks **Yes**; it is wrong.)* Two things in the query prove it is a **table-valued function**: it is given a **table alias** (`AS gdr`), and **individual columns are selected from that alias** (`gdr.[WWI Employee ID]`, `gdr.Employee`). A scalar function returns *one value* — it has no columns to alias and cannot appear as the right operand of `APPLY`. The community is clear on this too (+22, +10, +6 all answer No).

**2. It will run only once → No.** `APPLY` is a **correlated** operator: the doc describes it as invoking the right-hand table expression *"for each row of the left table expression"*. Its argument here is `e.[Employee Key]`, which differs per row — so the function runs once per employee.

**3. At least one output row per Employee row → Yes.** This is the difference between the two forms of APPLY:

| Form | Left rows with no function output |
| --- | --- |
| `CROSS APPLY` | **dropped** (inner-join semantics) |
| **`OUTER APPLY`** | **kept, with NULLs** (left-outer-join semantics) |

Because it is `OUTER APPLY`, an employee with no direct reports still produces one row, with NULL in the Direct Report columns. So every Employee row yields at least one output row.

FILTER (

questions.explanation:
**No.** The proposed line 4 is

```dax
NOT ( CALCULATE ( COUNTROWS ( 'Order Item' ) ) < 0 )
```

- **The result is wrong.** A row count is never negative, so `< 0` is always false and `NOT(false)` is always **true**. Every customer passes the filter, including those with no orders — which is precisely who the original `> 0` excluded.

You have a Fabric tenant.
You are creating a Fabric Data Factory pipeline.
You have a stored procedure that returns the number of active customers and their average sales for the current month.
You need to add an activity that will execute the stored procedure in a warehouse. The returned values must be available to the downstream
activities of the pipeline.

questions.explanation:
**Lookup** — the activity that both *runs* a stored procedure and *returns* its result set to the rest of the pipeline: *"Lookup activity reads and returns the content of a configuration file or table. It also returns the result of executing a query or stored procedure. The output can be a singleton value or an array of attributes, which can be consumed in a subsequent copy, transformation, or control flow activity."*

- **A Get metadata** – returns *metadata about a file or folder* (name, size, last modified, child items). It cannot execute a stored procedure.
- **B Copy data** – can call a stored procedure as a source, but it writes the rows to a sink instead of exposing them downstream.
- **D Append variable** – appends a value to an array variable; it executes nothing.

*(This question appears four times in the bank with different distractor sets — T1Q83, T1Q114, T1Q122, T1Q128. The answer is Lookup every time.)*

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse named Warehouse1. Warehouse1 contains a fact table named FactSales that has one billion
rows.
You run the following T-SQL statement.
CREATE TABLE test.FactSales AS CLONE OF dbo.FactSales;
For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

statements.text: A replica of dbo.FactSales is created in the test schema by copying the metadata only.
Additional schema changes to dbo.FactSales will also apply to test.FactSales.
Additional data changes to dbo.FactSales will also apply to test.FactSales.

questions.explanation:
**Yes — No — No.** Two documented properties of a Fabric table clone settle all three.

**1. Metadata only → Yes.** The `CREATE TABLE AS CLONE OF` reference is explicit: *"Creates a new table as a **zero-copy clone** of another table in Warehouse in Microsoft Fabric. **Only the metadata of the table is copied. The underlying data of the table, stored as parquet files, is not copied.**"* That is why a clone of a one-billion-row fact table is near-instantaneous.

**2 & 3. Later changes propagate → No, and No.** A clone is a point-in-time snapshot, not a link: *"Upon creation, a table clone is an **independent and separate** entity… Any changes made to the source table after the clone is created do not reflect in the clone, and vice versa."* This works because Parquet files are immutable — the clone simply keeps referencing the set of files that existed at clone time, while new writes to `dbo.FactSales` create new files that only its own log knows about. Schema changes (2) and data changes (3) are both invisible to the clone.

*Note:* one commenter argues all three are No, on the grounds that a clone "includes the data". It does make the data *visible*, but it does not **copy** it — which is precisely the wording of statement 1. The two other comments (+24, +6) and the answer key all give Yes/No/No.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse named DW1 and a lakehouse named LH1. DW1 contains a table named Sales.Product. LH1
contains a table named Sales.Orders.
You plan to schedule an automated process that will create a new point-in-time (PIT) table named Sales.ProductOrder in DW1. Sales.ProductOrder
will be built by using the results of a query that will join Sales.Product and Sales.Orders.
You need to ensure that the types of columns in Sales.ProductOrder match the column types in the source tables. The solution must minimize the
number of operations required to create the new table.
Which operation should you use?
questions.explanation:
**CTAS.** Three constraints, and only `CREATE TABLE AS SELECT` satisfies all of them:

- **The source is a join across two items.** `Sales.Product` is in the warehouse, `Sales.Orders` is in the lakehouse, and the new table is built *"by using the results of a query that will join"* them. CTAS takes an arbitrary `SELECT`, including a cross-item join.
- **Column types must match the source.** CTAS **derives the schema from the query's result set**, so the types come across automatically. There is no `CREATE TABLE` DDL to write and keep in sync.
- **Minimize the number of operations.** One statement creates and populates the table.

Rejected:
- **A INSERT INTO** – needs the table to exist first, so you would write the `CREATE TABLE` DDL yourself (hand-maintaining every data type) and then insert. Two operations, and the type-matching requirement becomes manual.
- **C CREATE TABLE AS CLONE OF** – clones a **single existing table**. It cannot take a query, let alone a join, and clones across items are not supported.
- **D CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW AS SELECT** – would not produce a *table*, and the requirement is a scheduled point-in-time snapshot. (Materialized views are also listed as unsupported in the Fabric Warehouse T-SQL surface area.)

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains two workspaces named Workspace1 and Workspace2 and a user named User1.
You need to ensure that User1 can perform the following tasks:
• Create a new domain.
• Create two subdomains named subdomain1 and subdomain2.
• Assign Workspace1 to subdomain1.
• Assign Workspace2 to subdomain2.
The solution must follow the principle of least privilege.
Which role should you assign to User1?
questions.explanation:
Least privilege usually pushes you down the role list — but here the **first** task sets a floor. The domains doc states it plainly: *"Only **Fabric admins** can create domains."* Nothing below that can do it, so the answer cannot be lower than **Fabric admin**.

Checked against all four tasks:

| Task | Minimum role |
| --- | --- |
| **Create a new domain** | **Fabric admin** |
| Create subdomains | Fabric admin *or* domain admin |
| Assign workspaces to a (sub)domain | Fabric admin, domain admin, or domain contributor |

- **A domain admin** – can create **subdomains** of a domain they already own and manage its workspaces, but cannot create the top-level domain in the first place. This is the near-miss, and 20% of the community picks it.
- **B domain contributor** – the weakest domain role: it can only assign workspaces it already administers to a domain.
- **D workspace Admin** – scoped to a single workspace; no domain rights at all.

*(Note that a Fabric admin would normally then **delegate** by assigning a domain admin — but the question asks which single role lets User1 do all four things.)*

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains three users named User1, User2, and User3. The tenant contains a security group named Group1. User1
and User3 are members of Group1.
The tenant contains the workspaces shown in the following table.
The tenant contains the domains shown in the following table.
User1 creates a new workspace named Workspace3.
You assign Domain1 as the default domain of Group1.
For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

statements.text: User2 is assigned the Contributor role for Workspace3.
User3 is assigned the Viewer role for Workspace3.
User3 is assigned the Contributor role for Workspace1.

questions.explanation:
**No — No — No.** The whole question turns on one fact: **domains do not grant workspace roles.**

What the setup actually does. Assigning **Domain1 as the *default domain* of Group1** means that when a member of Group1 creates a workspace, that workspace is **automatically associated with Domain1**. The doc describes it as a convenience for organising content: a default domain *"will automatically be assigned to workspaces created by members of that group"*. It is a **content-organisation** feature — it affects OneLake data hub filtering and domain-level governance, not who can open or edit anything.

Workspace access comes from exactly one place: an explicit role assignment (Admin / Member / Contributor / Viewer) on that workspace. So:

1. **User2 → Contributor on Workspace3? No.** User2 is not even in Group1, and nobody assigned them anything on Workspace3. (User2 is the admin of Workspace2 and of Domain2 — neither reaches Workspace3.)
2. **User3 → Viewer on Workspace3? No.** User3 *is* in Group1, so Workspace3 lands in Domain1 — but sharing a domain with a workspace confers no role in it. Only User1, who created Workspace3, is its admin.
3. **User3 → Contributor on Workspace1? No.** Workspace1's admin is User1. No role was granted to User3 or to Group1.

*Note:* one comment (+6) answers Yes to statement 2, reasoning that User3 "likely inherits" Viewer through the domain. There is no such inheritance; two other comments and the answer key all give No/No/No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
Row-level security in a Fabric warehouse is the standard SQL Server RLS mechanism, and it is built from exactly two objects:

1. **D — a FUNCTION.** An **inline table-valued function** that encodes the filter logic and acts as the *security predicate*. For "users see only their own data" it typically compares a column to the caller:

```sql
CREATE FUNCTION Security.tvf_securitypredicate(@SalesRep AS nvarchar(50))
    RETURNS TABLE WITH SCHEMABINDING
AS
    RETURN SELECT 1 AS Result WHERE @SalesRep = USER_NAME();
```

2. **E — a SECURITY POLICY.** The object that **binds** the predicate to the table. Without it the function is just a function and filters nothing:

```sql
CREATE SECURITY POLICY SalesFilter
ADD FILTER PREDICATE Security.tvf_securitypredicate(SalesRep) ON dbo.Table1
WITH (STATE = ON);
```

Rejected:
- **A DATABASE ROLE** – the 27% runner-up. Roles are a perfectly normal way to *organise* who the predicate should apply to, and RLS is often combined with them — but they are **optional**. The requirement here is per-*user* filtering, which `USER_NAME()` handles directly. The two objects RLS cannot exist without are the function and the policy.
- **B STORED PROCEDURE** – a security predicate must be an inline TVF; a procedure cannot be used.
- **C CONSTRAINT** – constrains what can be *written*, not what can be *read*.

refs.t: Row-level security in Fabric Data Warehousing

You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1. Lakehouse1 contains a table named Table1.
Table1 contains the following data.
You need to perform the following actions:
• Load the data from Table1 into a star schema.
• Create a product dimension table named DimProduct and a fact table named FactSales.
Which three columns should you include in DimProduct?

semanticVisuals.title: Lakehouse table columns
rows: Contains a unique ID for each transaction
Contains the date of each transaction
Contains a unique ID for each product
Contains a descriptive attribute that describes the color of each product
Contains a unique name for each product
Contains the sales amount of each transaction

questions.explanation:
Split the columns by what each one *describes*:

| Column | Describes | Goes to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `TransactionID` | the transaction | FactSales (degenerate dimension) |
| `Date` | when the transaction happened | FactSales |
| **`ProductID`** | **a unique ID for each product** | **DimProduct** (key) |
| **`ProductName`** | **a unique name for each product** | **DimProduct** (attribute) |
| **`ProductColor`** | **a descriptive attribute of the product** | **DimProduct** (attribute) |
| `SalesAmount` | the money for the transaction | FactSales (measure) |

So DimProduct = **ProductColor, ProductID, ProductName** — **A**. A dimension holds the *who / what* context; the fact table holds the numeric measures and the event keys.

- **B** and **D** include `SalesAmount`, a **measure**. Measures belong in the fact table; putting one in a dimension would fix the amount per product rather than per transaction.
- **C** includes `Date` and `TransactionID`, both attributes of the *transaction*, not of the product.

questions.stem:
You have a Microsoft Power Bl project that contains a file named definition.pbir. definition.pbir contains the following JSON.
For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

statements.text: definition.pbir is in the PBIR-Legacy format.
The semantic model referenced by definition.pbir is located in the Power BI service.
When the related report is opened, Power BI Desktop will open the semantic model in full edit mode.

semanticVisuals.title: definition.pbir — original JSON

questions.explanation:
**Yes — No — Yes.** The file is

```json
{
  "version": "1.0",
  "datasetReference": {
    "byPath": { "path": "../Sales.Dataset" },
    "byConnection": null
  }
}
```

**1. PBIR-Legacy → Yes.** *(The PDF answer-key image marks **No**; it is wrong.)* The `version` property is precisely what declares the report definition format, and the doc gives the mapping as a table:

| Version | Supported formats |
| --- | --- |
| **1.0** | **Report definition must be stored as PBIR-Legacy in the `report.json` file.** |
| 4.0 or higher | Report definition can be stored as PBIR-Legacy (`report.json`) **or** PBIR (`\definition` folder). |

At `"version": "1.0"` the report definition *must* be PBIR-Legacy — there is no other option at that version. (Microsoft's own example of the current format uses `"version": "4.0"`.) The highest-voted comment asserts that *"1.0 isn't legacy format … the version would be blank if it was legacy"*, which the documented table contradicts; a later comment answers Yes.

**2. The model is in the Power BI service → No.** The reference is **`byPath`**, a *relative path to a local folder* (`../Sales.Dataset`), and `byConnection` is explicitly `null`. `byConnection` is the one that *"specifies the connection to a semantic model in a Fabric workspace by using a connection string"* — it is not in use here.

**3. Desktop opens the model in full edit mode → Yes.** Straight from the doc, on `byPath`: *"When used, Power BI Desktop **also opens the semantic model in full edit mode**."* The contrast is stated in the next line: *"When a `byConnection` reference is used, Power BI Desktop doesn't open the semantic model in edit mode."*

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1.
You plan to deploy a semantic model named Model1 by using the XMLA endpoint.
You need to optimize the deployment of Model1. The solution must minimize how long it takes to deploy Model1.
What should you do in Workspace1?

options.text: Select Small semantic model storage format.
Select Users can edit data models in the Power BI service.
Set Enable Cache for Shortcuts to On.
Select Large semantic model storage format.

questions.explanation:
**Large semantic model storage format.** Microsoft recommends it specifically for XMLA deployments, regardless of model size: *"If you're planning to use XMLA endpoint-based tools for semantic model **write** operations, be sure to enable the setting, **even for semantic models that you wouldn't necessarily characterize as a large semantic model**. When enabled, the large semantic model storage format can **improve XMLA write operations performance**."*

The reason is how the model is persisted: the large format stores the model in **premium files** with incremental, per-object writes, instead of serialising the whole model on every write. Deployments touch far less data and finish faster.

- **B Users can edit data models in the Power BI service** – enables web modelling. Nothing to do with XMLA deployment speed.
- **C Enable Cache for Shortcuts** – a OneLake shortcut caching setting for external data reads. Unrelated to semantic models.

questions.stem:
You have a Microsoft Power BI project that contains a semantic model.
You plan to use Azure DevOps for version control.
You need to modify the .gitignore file to prevent the data values from the data sources from being pushed to the repository.
Which file should you reference?
questions.explanation:
**`cache.abf`.** In a Power BI project's `.SemanticModel` folder, `cache.abf` is the **Analysis Services backup file** holding the model's **cached data** — the actual imported rows from your data sources. It is binary, it can be very large, and it is the one file that would push real data values into the repository. `.gitignore` it.

What the others are:
- **D `model.bim`** – the model **definition** in TMSL/JSON: tables, columns, measures, relationships. Metadata only, and it is exactly what you *want* under version control.
- **A `unappliedChanges.json`** – pending edits not yet applied to the model. Metadata.
- **C `localSettings.json`** – per-user, per-machine settings. It *should* also be excluded — and the doc notes *"By default, Git ignores this file"* — but it holds preferences, not data values, so it does not answer the question as asked.

The default `.gitignore` that Power BI Desktop generates for a project already excludes `cache.abf` and `.pbi/localSettings.json` for these reasons.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a lakehouse named LH1.
You need to deploy a new semantic model. The solution must meet the following requirements:
• Support complex calculated columns that include aggregate functions, calculated tables, and Multidimensional Expressions (MDX) user
hierarchies.
• Minimize page rendering times.
How should you configure the model? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
**Import — On.**

**Mode — Import.** The first requirement lists three things that **Direct Lake does not support**. From the storage-mode comparison table in the Direct Lake docs:

| Capability | Direct Lake | Import | DirectQuery |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Calculated columns with aggregate functions | **No** | **Yes** | No |
| Calculated tables | **No** | **Yes** | No |
| MDX user hierarchies | **No** | **Yes** | Yes |

Only **Import** answers Yes to all three. (Direct Lake carves out a narrow exception for calculation groups, what-if parameters and field parameters, which implicitly create calculated tables — but not for the general case the requirement describes.) DirectQuery fails on calculated columns and calculated tables, and is the slowest of the three anyway.

**Query Caching — On.** The second requirement is *"minimize page rendering times"*. Query caching stores the results of a report's queries so that subsequent loads are served from the cache instead of re-querying the model — it is the setting whose stated purpose is faster report loads. *Capacity default* leaves it to chance; *Off* forgoes the benefit. It is available on Premium/Embedded and applies to **Import** models, which fits the mode chosen above.

questions.stem:
You have the following KQL query.
For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

statements.text: The query excludes sales that have a Status of Cancelled.
The query calculates the total sales of each product category for the last 30 days.
The query includes product categories that have had zero sales during the last 30 days.

semanticVisuals.title: Original KQL aggregation and filtering query
semanticVisuals.content:
Sales
| where Status != "Cancelled"
| where OrderDate >= ago(30d)
| summarize TotalSales = sum(SalesAmount) by ProductCategory
| where TotalSales > 0

questions.explanation:
**Yes — Yes — No.** Read the KQL one operator at a time:

```kusto
Sales
| where Status != "Cancelled"                              // 1
| where OrderDate >= ago(30d)                              // 2
| summarize TotalSales = sum(SalesAmount) by ProductCategory   // 2
| where TotalSales > 0                                     // 3
```

**1. Excludes cancelled sales → Yes.** `!=` is "not equal to", so `where Status != "Cancelled"` keeps every row whose status is anything other than Cancelled.

**2. Total sales per product category for the last 30 days → Yes.** `ago(30d)` returns the timestamp 30 days before now, so `OrderDate >= ago(30d)` keeps the last 30 days. `summarize sum(SalesAmount) by ProductCategory` then totals within each category. Both halves of the statement hold.

**3. Includes categories with zero sales → No.** Two independent reasons:
- `summarize … by ProductCategory` only produces groups for categories that **have rows** in the filtered input. A category with no sales in the window contributes no rows, so no group.
- The final `| where TotalSales > 0` explicitly discards anything that totalled zero (or less, e.g. a refund-only category).

*(One commenter reads statement 2 as No; the last line filters *after* the summarize, so it does not change what is being calculated — it only trims the output. The answer key and the other comments give Yes/Yes/No.)*

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric warehouse that contains a table named SalesOrderDetail, SalesOrderDetail contains three columns named OrderQty, ProductID
and SalesOrderlD. SalesOrderDetail contains one row per combination of SalesOrderlD and ProductID.
You need to calculate the proportion of the total quantity of each sales order represented by each product within the sales order.
Which T-SQL statement should you run?
A.
B.
C.
D.

options.code:
SELECT SalesOrderID, ProductID, OrderQty,
 CAST(1. * OrderQty / SUM(OrderQty) OVER(PARTITION BY ProductID) * 100
 AS DECIMAL(5,2)) AS PercentbyProductID
FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail;

SELECT SalesOrderID, ProductID, OrderQty,
 CAST(1. * OrderQty / SUM(OrderQty) OVER(ORDER BY SalesOrderID) * 100
 AS DECIMAL(5,2)) AS PercentbyProductID
FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail;

SELECT SalesOrderID, ProductID, OrderQty,
 CAST(1. * OrderQty / SUM(OrderQty) OVER(ORDER BY ProductID) * 100
 AS DECIMAL(5,2)) AS PercentbyProductID
FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail;

SELECT SalesOrderID, ProductID, OrderQty,
 CAST(1. * OrderQty / SUM(OrderQty) OVER(PARTITION BY SalesOrderID) * 100
 AS DECIMAL(5,2)) AS PercentbyProductID
FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail;

questions.explanation:
The requirement is *"the proportion of the total quantity of **each sales order** represented by each product **within the sales order**"*. The denominator is therefore the total for the **sales order**, which means the window must be partitioned by `SalesOrderID`:

```sql
SELECT SalesOrderID, ProductID, OrderQty
  , CAST(1. * OrderQty / SUM(OrderQty) OVER (PARTITION BY SalesOrderID) * 100 AS DECIMAL(5,2)) AS PercentbyProductID
FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail;
```

That is **D**. Two details are doing quiet work: `PARTITION BY` with **no** `ORDER BY` gives a window over the *entire* partition (the whole order), which is what a denominator needs; and `1. *` forces decimal arithmetic so the division does not truncate to an integer.

- **A — `PARTITION BY ProductID`.** Divides by the total quantity of that **product across all orders**. Right function, wrong grouping key — the classic trap.
- **B — `ORDER BY SalesOrderID`** and **C — `ORDER BY ProductID`.** `OVER` with an `ORDER BY` and no frame clause defaults to `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, making `SUM` a **running total** rather than a partition total. The denominator would grow row by row, which is not a proportion of anything.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1. Workspace1 contains a warehouse named DW1. DW1 contains two
tables named Employees and Sales. All users have read access to Dw1.
You need to implement access controls to meet the following requirements:
• For the Sales table, ensure that the users can see only the sales data from their respective region.
• For the Employees table, restrict access to all Personally Identifiable Information (PII).
• Maintain access to unrestricted data for all the users.
What should you use for each table? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

blanks.label: Employees:  (restrict access to all PII, keep the rest visible)
Sales:  (users see only their own region’s sales)

questions.explanation:
**Column-level security — Row-level security.** Two requirements that differ along different axes of the table:

| Requirement | Restricts | Feature |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Employees: *"restrict access to all **Personally Identifiable Information**"* | specific **columns** | **Column-level security (CLS)** |
| Sales: *"see only the sales data from their respective **region**"* | specific **rows** | **Row-level security (RLS)** |

- **CLS** — *"allows you to restrict column access to protect sensitive data"*. PII lives in named columns (SSN, date of birth, home address), so you deny those columns and the rest of the Employees table stays readable. This also satisfies *"maintain access to unrestricted data for all the users"*.
- **RLS** — *"control access to rows in a database table … you can ensure that workers access only those data rows that are pertinent to their department"*. Region is a row attribute, so a filter predicate on it is the right tool.

Rejected:
- **Item permissions** and **Workspace permissions** are all-or-nothing on the whole item or workspace. Revoking either would remove access to the unrestricted data too, breaking the third requirement — and the stem already says *"all users have read access to DW1"*.

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1 and a user named User1. User1 is assigned the Contributor role for
Workspace1.
You plan to configure Workspace1 to use an Azure DevOps repository for version control.

Two tenant settings gate Git commits from a workspace:

- **D — *Users can synchronize workspace items with their Git repositories*.** The master switch for Fabric Git integration. Without it there is no Connect/Commit/Update at all.
- **C — *Users can create Fabric items*.** Committing writes item definitions, and syncing back creates and updates items in the workspace. Without the right to create Fabric items the user cannot complete the operation.

Rejected:
- **A — *Users can sync workspace items with GitHub repositories*.** The deliberate trap. The scenario says **Azure DevOps**, which is covered by the generic *Git repositories* setting (D). GitHub has its own **separate** tenant switch, and turning it on does nothing for an Azure Repos connection. "Azure DevOps uses Git" ≠ "Azure DevOps is GitHub".
- **B — *Users can create and use Data workflows*.** Apache Airflow jobs. Unrelated.

Note that User1 already has the **Contributor** workspace role, which is the minimum role that can commit — so the remaining gaps are the two tenant settings.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1. Workspace1 contains a data pipeline named Pipeline1 and a lakehouse
named Lakehouse1.
You perform the following actions:
• Create a workspace named Workspace2.
• Create a deployment pipeline named DeployPipeline1 that will deploy items from Workspace1 to Workspace2.
• Add a folder named Folder1 to Workspace1.
• Move Lakehouse1 to Folder1.
• Run DeployPipeline1.
Which structure will Workspace2 have when DeployPipeline1 is complete?
questions.explanation:
**`\Pipeline1` and `\Folder1\Lakehouse1`.** Two rules combine.

**1. Folders travel with their items.** The doc: *"In Deployment pipelines, **folders are considered part of an item's name** (an item name includes its full path). When an item is deployed, after its path was changed (moved from folder A to folder B, for example), then Deployment pipelines applies this change to its paired item during deployment… **If folder B doesn't exist in the stage we're deploying to, it's created in its workspace first.**"*

Lakehouse1 was moved into `Folder1` **before** the deployment ran, so its full name is now `Folder1\Lakehouse1`. Workspace2 gets `Folder1` created for it, with Lakehouse1 inside.

**2. Pipeline1 never moved.** It is still at the root of Workspace1, so it deploys to the root of Workspace2 — and it *does* deploy; Data pipelines are a supported item type.

Rejected:
- **D `\Folder1\Lakehouse1`** only – drops Pipeline1 entirely. Nothing excluded it from the deployment.
- **B `\Pipeline1` `\Lakehouse1`** – assumes folders are ignored by deployment. The doc says the opposite.
- **A** – puts Pipeline1 in Folder1 too, but it was never moved there.

questions.stem:
Your company has a finance department.
You have a Fabric tenant, an Azure Storage account named storage1, and a Microsoft Entra group named Group1. Group1 contains the users in the
finance department.
You need to create a new workspace named Workspace1 in the tenant. The solution must meet the following requirements:
• Ensure that the finance department users can create and edit items in Workspace1.
• Ensure that Workspace1 can securely access storage1 to read and write data.
• Ensure that you are the only admin of Workspace1.
• Minimize administrative effort.
You create Workspace1.
Which two actions should you perform next? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: Assign the Contributor role to Group1.
Assign the Admin role to yourself.
Assign the Contributor role to each finance department user.

questions.explanation:
Four requirements, and two actions cover them:

- **A — assign the Contributor role to Group1.** *"Finance department users can create and edit items"* → **Contributor** is the lowest workspace role that can create and edit. Assigning it to **Group1** rather than to individuals satisfies *"minimize administrative effort"*: new starters inherit access through group membership with no extra work.
- **B — create a workspace identity.** *"Workspace1 can **securely** access storage1 to read and write data"* → a **workspace identity** is the Microsoft Entra service principal automatically created for the workspace; you grant it a role on `storage1` and Fabric items authenticate with it. No keys, no SAS tokens, no stored credentials — that is the "securely" part.

Rejected:
- **C — assign the Admin role to yourself.** Unnecessary: *"The deploying/creating user automatically becomes … the only admin of the new workspace."* You created Workspace1, so you already are its admin — and the requirement is that you remain the **only** one.
- **D — assign Contributor to each finance user individually.** Same end state as A but the maximum administrative effort, and it drifts out of date as the department changes.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains the workspaces shown in the following table.
You have a deployment pipeline named Pipeline1 that deploys items from Workspace_DEV to Workspace_TEST. In Pipeline1, all items that have
matching names are paired.
You deploy the contents of Workspace_DEV to Workspace_TEST by using Pipeline1.
What will the contents of Workspace_TEST be once the deployment is complete?

options.text: Lakehouse1 - Lakehouse2 - Notebook1 - Notebook2 - Pipeline1 - SemanticModel1

questions.explanation:
Deployment **adds and overwrites; it never deletes**. The doc: *"the items being copied from the source stage overwrite the paired item in the stage you're in according to the pairing rules. **Items that don't exist in the source stage remain as is.**"*

Work it through. Only items with **matching names** are paired:

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lakehouse1 | — | no | **Lakehouse1** (new) |
| — | Lakehouse2 | no | Lakehouse2 (untouched) |
| Notebook1 | — | no | **Notebook1** (new) |
| — | Notebook2 | no | Notebook2 (untouched) |
| Pipeline1 | — | no | **Pipeline1** (new) |
| SemanticModel1 | SemanticModel1 | **yes** | SemanticModel1 (overwritten) |

The result is the **union**: Lakehouse1, Lakehouse2, Notebook1, Notebook2, Pipeline1, SemanticModel1 — **A**.

- **B** is Workspace_DEV's contents, as if deployment replaced the whole workspace. It does not.
- **C / D** drop the newly deployed items.

*(Note "Pipeline1" here is a **data pipeline item** in Workspace_DEV, distinct from the deployment pipeline doing the deploying — a confusing naming choice in the question, and one commenter is caught by it.)*

questions.explanation:
**Yes — No — No. The PDF answer-key image (No / Yes / Yes) is wrong on all three**, and the documentation settles each one outright.

**1. DF1 (a Dataflow **Gen1**) will be deployed → Yes.** The supported-items list carries two separate entries: **"Dataflows gen2"** under *Data Factory items*, and plain **"Dataflow *(preview)*"** under *Power BI items* — the latter is Gen1. The dataflow-limitations section confirms Gen1 goes through the pipeline by noting a Gen1-specific caveat: *"Incremental refresh settings aren't copied in Gen 1."* You would not document a copy limitation for an item type that is never deployed.

**2. Data from Model1 will be deployed → No.** From *Item properties that are not copied*: *"**Data — Data isn't copied. > - Role assignment
> - **Refresh schedule**
> - Data source credentials
> - Query caching settings
> - Endorsement settings

The data has the following characteristics:
• Each customer is assigned a unique CustomerID value.
• Each customer is associated to a single SalesRegion value.
• Each customer is associated to a single CustomerAddress value.
• The Customer table contains 5 million rows.
• All foreign key values are non-null.

must minimize query processing time and resources.
How should you complete the T-SQL statement? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Candidate constraint: every customer has exactly one CustomerAddress row with AddressType=Main Office, its AddressID resolves uniquely, and every SalesRegion foreign key resolves to one row. This task asks for correct joins, not a guaranteed optimizer performance ranking.

semanticVisuals.title: Denormalized customer dimension view — original template
semanticVisuals.content:
CREATE VIEW DimCustomer AS
SELECT C.CustomerID, C.CustomerName, C.CompanyName,
       SR.SalesRegion, A.City, A.StateProvince,
       A.CountryRegion, A.PostalCode
FROM SalesLT.Customer C
[Dropdown 1] SalesLT.SalesRegion SR
    ON C.SalesRegionID = SR.SalesRegionID
INNER JOIN SalesLT.CustomerAddress CA
    ON CA.CustomerID = C.CustomerID
INNER JOIN SalesLT.Address A
    ON [Dropdown 2]
WHERE CA.AddressType = 'Main Office';

questions.stem:
You have a query in Microsoft Power BI Desktop that contains two columns named Order_Date and Shipping_Date.
You need to create a column that will calculate the number of days between Order_Date and Shipping_Date for each row.
Which Power Query function should you use?
questions.explanation:
Subtracting two dates in Power Query yields a **duration** value, and `Duration.Days` extracts the whole number of days from it:

```m
Duration.Days([Shipping_Date] - [Order_Date])
```

- **C `Duration.From`** – *converts* a value to a duration. It does not give you a day count, and the subtraction has already produced a duration anyway.
- **D `Date.AddDays`** – shifts a date forward or back by N days. That is the inverse operation.
- **A `DateTime.LocalNow`** – returns the current local date and time. Nothing to do with the gap between two columns.

questions.stem:
You have a Microsoft Power BI semantic model that contains a measure named TotalSalesAmount. TotalSalesAmount returns a sales revenue
amount that is translated into a selected currency.
You need to ensure that the value returned by TotalSalesAmount is formatted to use the correct currency symbol.
What should you include in the solution?
questions.explanation:
A **dynamic format string** lets a measure decide its own formatting at evaluation time: *"With dynamic format strings for measures, you can determine how measures appear in visuals by **conditionally applying a format string with a separate DAX formula**."*

That is exactly the requirement — the measure already returns a value translated into the selected currency, so the format string must follow the same selection:

```dax
SWITCH (
    SELECTEDVALUE ( Currency[Code] ),
    "USD", "$#,##0.00",
    "EUR", "€#,##0.00",
    "GBP", "£#,##0.00",
    "#,##0.00"
)
```

A static format string on the measure could only ever show one symbol.

- **A a field parameter** – lets report users swap which *fields* a visual shows. It does not control formatting.
- **B a linguistic schema** – vocabulary for Q&A natural-language queries.
- **D the WINDOW DAX function** – returns a subset of rows from a table for window calculations. Unrelated to formatting.

questions.stem:
You plan to use Fabric to store data.
You need to create a data store that supports the following:
• Writing data by using T-SQL
• Multi-table transactions
• Dynamic data masking
Which type of data store should you create?
questions.explanation:
Only the **warehouse** has all three capabilities:

| Requirement | Warehouse | Lakehouse | KQL database |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Write data by using T-SQL** | ✔ | ✘ — its SQL analytics endpoint is **read-only**; you write with Spark | ✘ — KQL, not T-SQL |
| **Multi-table transactions** | ✔ — full ACID `BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK` across tables | ✘ — Delta transactions are per-table | ✘ |
| **Dynamic data masking** | ✔ | ✘ | ✘ |

Multi-table transaction support is the clearest discriminator: it is a documented warehouse feature, and Delta Lake (and therefore the lakehouse) commits one table at a time. Dynamic data masking is documented as *"Applies to: SQL analytics endpoint and **Warehouse** in Microsoft Fabric"*.

- **D a semantic model** is not a data store at all — it is an analytics layer over one.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1. Workspace1 uses the Pro license mode and contains a semantic model
named Model1.
You have an Azure DevOps organization.
You need to enable version control for Workspace1. The solution must ensure that Model1 is added to the repository.

Configure branch policies in Azure DevOps.
Assign Workspace1 to a Fabric capacity.

targets.answer: Assign Workspace1 to a Fabric capacity.

questions.explanation:
**Assign to a Fabric capacity → Connect to a Git provider → Sync with the repository.**

1. **Assign Workspace1 to a Fabric capacity.** The workspace is on the **Pro** license mode, and Git integration has a hard prerequisite: *"To access the Git integration feature, **you need a Fabric capacity**."* Nothing else can happen first.
2. **Connect Workspace1 to a Git provider.** *Workspace settings → Git integration* → choose Azure DevOps, then the organization, project, repository and branch.
3. **Sync Workspace1 with the repository.** Connecting establishes the link; the initial **commit/sync** is what actually writes the workspace items — including **Model1** — into the repo. Without it the requirement *"ensure that Model1 is added to the repository"* is unmet.

Rejected:
- **Create a deployment pipeline** – deployment pipelines move content **between stages** (CI/CD release). They are not version control, and nothing lands in Azure Repos.
- **Configure branch policies in Azure DevOps** – a governance nicety (required reviewers, build validation). It does not enable version control or add Model1 to the repo.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1 and a user named User1. Workspace1 contains a warehouse named DW1.
You share DW1 with User1 and assign User1 the default permissions for DW1.

Connecting is all it allows. Querying data requires more:

| Capability | Permission needed | Granted by default? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Connect to the SQL endpoint** | Read | **yes** |
| Read data from the tables | **ReadData** | no |
| Build reports on the default semantic model | **Build** | no |
| Read the underlying Parquet in OneLake | **ReadAll** (OneLake/Spark) | no |

So **C**. Options **B**, **A** and **D** each map to one of the *additional* permissions that were not selected — which is exactly the distinction the question is testing.
